### Description

Since Keycloak 26.8.0, `GET /admin/realms/{realm}/clients/{id}/client-secret` and `.../client-secret/rotated` require `manage-clients`. (See Upgradeing Guide: [Client secret no longer returned for view-only client permissions](https://www.keycloak.org/docs/26.8.1/upgrading/#client-secret-no-longer-returned-for-view-only-client-permissions))

A caller with only `view-clients` gets HTTP 403 when try to read client secrets. No role and no fine-grained admin permissions (FGAP) scope lets a caller read a client secret without the right to create, change and delete clients. The `Clients` resource type in FGAP V2 offers only `view`, `manage`, `map-roles`, `map-roles-client-scope` and `map-roles-composite`.

Please add a permission that only reads client secrets. Two possible shapes:

- a `realm-management` role, for example `view-client-secrets`, for a service account that reads the secrets of every client in a realm;
- a scope on the `Clients` resource type in FGAP V2, for example `view-secret`, for access limited to selected clients.


### Value Proposition

A secret broker needs to read client secrets and nothing else. Example: the HashiCorp Vault plugin [vault-plugin-secrets-keycloak](https://github.com/Serviceware/vault-plugin-secrets-keycloak) serves Keycloak client secrets to applications. It logs in as a service account and reads each secret from the client-secret endpoint. Its [Terraform module](https://github.com/Serviceware/terraform-vaultkeycloak-keycloak-client/blob/main/main.tf) grants that service account `view-clients` only. Since 26.8.0 the plugin gets HTTP 403 and serves no secrets.

The only fix today is `manage-clients`, as the upgrade note recommends. That turns a read-only integration into a full client administrator: it can create clients, change redirect URIs, regenerate secrets and delete clients. A read-only permission keeps the least-privilege goal of #49220 for the integrations that the change broke.

### Goals

- A caller with the new permission and without `manage-clients` gets HTTP 200 and the secret from `GET .../clients/{id}/client-secret` and `.../client-secret/rotated`.
- The same caller gets HTTP 403 from every endpoint that creates, updates or deletes a client, and from `POST .../client-secret`.
- An administrator can grant the permission to a service account, as a realm role or as an FGAP V2 scope limited to selected clients.
- The upgrade note names the permission as the alternative to `manage-clients` for automation that reads secrets.

### Non-Goals

- Regenerating secrets or managing other client credentials (#45094, #39482).
- Unmasking `secret` in the representations from `GET .../clients` and `GET .../clients/{id}`. They can stay masked.
- Changing how Keycloak stores secrets (#15567).

### Discussion

_No response_

### Notes

- #40646 asked for a separate role or permission for the secret endpoint. 26.8.0 delivered the masking part of that request. This issue is the follow-up that a maintainer asked for there on 2026-09-21.
- Verified against the 26.8.0 tag and `main` on 2026-10-15: the GET endpoint requires `manage`, and the FGAP V2 schema has no secret scope.
- The long-term plan in #49220, to return the secret only at creation, would end this use case. Please consider secret brokers in that design.

## Describe the bug

The fix for CVE-2026-18217 ([#51781](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/51781)) changed `BaseSAML2BindingBuilder.generateRedirectUri()` to use `replaceQueryParam()` for `SAMLRequest`, `SAMLResponse`, and `RelayState`, preventing an attacker-supplied duplicate from surviving in the redirect URL. However, the `SigAlg` and `Signature` parameters are still added with `queryParam()` (append) instead of `replaceQueryParam()` (replace). When a client has a wildcard redirect URL, an attacker-supplied `SigAlg` or `Signature` parameter in the URL survives alongside Keycloak's own value, producing duplicate query parameters in the redirect sent to the service provider.

No authentication bypass has been demonstrated through SigAlg/Signature duplication alone. The impact is limited to signature verification failures at service providers that select the attacker's value (first occurrence), causing a failed login for the affected user.

## Version

Keycloak <= 26.8.1 (all builds containing the CVE-2026-18217 fix)

## Expected behavior

`SigAlg` and `Signature` should use `replaceQueryParam()` consistent with the other SAML redirect parameters, ensuring only one instance of each parameter appears in the final redirect URL.

## Actual behavior

`SigAlg` and `Signature` are appended with `queryParam()`, so attacker-supplied duplicates in the original URL survive alongside Keycloak's values. For example, a redirect URL containing `SigAlg=EVIL` results in two `SigAlg` parameters in the final URL.

## How to Reproduce?

## Describe the bug

The SSF transmitter's receiver-driven `POST /realms/{realm}/ssf/transmitter/subjects/remove` endpoint unconditionally clears the `ssf.notify.<clientId>` user attribute, including when it holds the administrator's explicit `"false"` exclusion marker set via the admin console's "Ignore" action.

After the marker is cleared, the same receiver can immediately re-add the subject via `POST /subjects/add`, which succeeds under the default `AUTHENTICATED` policy because the exclusion check in `mayAddUser()` no longer sees the `"false"` marker. This defeats the protection added by PR #53765 (fix for #53695), which was specifically built to prevent receivers from overriding an administrator's explicit "Ignore" decision.

The bug exists only in current main — the hardening it bypasses (#53765) has not yet shipped in a released version. SSF is an experimental feature.

## Version

Keycloak main @ 8a081db466da (2026-10-14). SSF is experimental (`--features=ssf`).

## Expected behavior

A receiver-driven remove should not lift an administrator's explicit "Ignore" exclusion. The `ssf.notify.<clientId>=false` marker should be preserved, and a subsequent receiver-driven add should remain blocked, matching the documented guarantee: "An explicit exclusion always wins: only an admin add can lift it."

## Actual behavior

`SubjectManagementService.unregisterSubjectForNotification()` calls `SsfNotifyAttributes.clearForUser()`, which unconditionally removes the attribute — including the admin's `"false"` exclusion marker. After removal, `mayAddUser()` no longer sees an exclusion, and the receiver can re-subscribe the ignored user to receive their security events (credential changes, session revocations, account state changes).

## Acknowledgement

Thank you to Irhas Abdul Rosyid for reporting this issue. As SSF is an experimental feature and the prior related issue (#53695) was handled as a public weakness without a CVE, this is treated consistently as a weakness and handled publicly.

## Describe the bug

When CRL checking is enabled in the X.509 client-certificate authenticator, the LDAP branch of the CRL loader reads the `certificateRevocationList;binary` attribute from an attacker-chosen LDAP server with no size limit. The CRL Distribution Point URL comes from the presented client certificate, so a single unauthenticated request can drive an arbitrarily large read into the JVM heap.

The HTTP/HTTPS branch already bounds the response with `SafeInputStream` (10 MB limit, added in PR #53697 / issue #52063). The LDAP branch was not hardened — JNDI buffers the entire LDAP message before Keycloak's code processes it.

Additionally, the parsed CRL is cached by `InfinispanCrlStorageProvider` before its signature is verified. When the CRL has no `nextUpdate`, the entry is stored with no lifespan (cached indefinitely). The cache is bounded by entry count only, never by size, so a few oversized CRLs can permanently exhaust heap until the cache is cleared or the server is restarted.

## Version

Keycloak 26.8.0 and main @ c7de391.

## Expected behavior

The LDAP CRL loader should apply the same size bound (`SafeInputStream` / `getMaxConsumedResponseSize()`) as the HTTP branch. The CRL cache should also enforce a size bound or a maximum lifespan to prevent persistent memory exhaustion.

## Actual behavior

A single unauthenticated request presenting a certificate with an LDAP CRL Distribution Point pointing to an attacker-controlled LDAP server causes an unbounded memory read. The oversized CRL is then cached indefinitely, making the memory exhaustion persistent across requests without a server restart or explicit cache clear.

## Acknowledgement

Thank you to Robin Marchand for reporting this issue. As this is the LDAP-side counterpart to a previously fixed HTTP-side issue (#52063) and follows the same handling pattern, this is considered a weakness and handled publicly.

### Before reporting an issue

- [x] I have read and understood the above terms for submitting issues, and I understand that my issue may be closed without action if I do not follow them.

### Area

oidc

### Describe the bug

The `AccessTokenContext` constructor checks `grantType` twice and never checks `rawTokenId`:

```java
Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null grantType not allowed");
Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");
```

A null `rawTokenId` is therefore accepted. The constructor is a `@JsonCreator`, so the value can also come from deserialized token context JSON. The null is later concatenated into the encoded token id in `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider`, where it appears as the literal string `null` instead of failing at construction.

### Version

26.8.1

### Regression

- [ ] The issue is a regression

### Expected behavior

Constructing an `AccessTokenContext` with a null `rawTokenId` throws `NullPointerException` with the message `Null rawTokenId not allowed`, like the other three arguments.

### Actual behavior

The constructor succeeds and stores the null `rawTokenId`.

### How to Reproduce?

```java
new AccessTokenContext(
        AccessTokenContext.SessionType.ONLINE,
        AccessTokenContext.TokenType.REGULAR,
        "ac",
        null);
```

No exception is thrown.

### Anything else?

A fix with tests is in #53990.

### Description

`DenylistPasswordPolicyProviderFactory.FileBasedPasswordDenylist.loadFromPlaintext` reads a plaintext denylist file twice:

1. `countPasswordsInDenylistFile` counts the lines, which is used to size the `BloomFilter`.
2. A second pass inserts the passwords.

`buildBloomFile`, which backs `kc.sh tools build-password-denylist`, uses the same two passes and counts with `Files.lines().count()`.

The counting pass uses `BufferedReader.lines().count()`. This decodes the entire file as UTF-8 and allocates a `String` for each line, then discards it. The method contains this TODO:

```java
/*
 * TODO find a more efficient way to determine the password count,
 * e.g. require a header-line in the password-denylist file
 */
```

Proposed change: count lines by scanning the raw bytes for `\n` and `\r`. In UTF-8, these byte values never occur inside a multi-byte sequence. A byte scan can therefore produce the same count as `BufferedReader`:

- `\n`, `\r` and `\r\n` are each treated as one line terminator.
- A final line without a terminator is counted.

### Value Proposition

The change reduces the time spent counting lines when a plaintext denylist is loaded, both on first use and on reload (#47163). It also applies to `buildBloomFile`. The file format, configuration and behaviour stay the same.

Measurements were taken on a macOS laptop under moderate background load. Absolute times vary between runs; the ratios were stable.

**Run 1:** [`xato-net-10-million-passwords.txt`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/danielmiessler/SecLists/master/Passwords/Common-Credentials/xato-net-10-million-passwords.txt) (5,189,454 lines, 46 MB, ASCII, `\n` line endings; the same list as in #47356). Three rounds in one JVM.

| | `BufferedReader.lines().count()` | byte scan |
|---|---|---|
| counting pass, cold (first run in a fresh JVM) | 219 ms | 90 ms |
| counting pass within load (3 rounds) | 221 / 181 / 193 ms | 88 / 86 / 61 ms |

**Run 2:** synthetic list of 5,000,000 random passwords (`Pw` + a base-36 random long, 73 MB, `\n` line endings). Three rounds in one JVM.

| | `BufferedReader.lines().count()` | byte scan |
|---|---|---|
| counting pass, warm (best of 5) | 162 ms | 31 ms |
| counting pass, cold (first run in a fresh JVM) | 241 ms | 100 ms |
| counting pass within load (3 rounds) | 247 / 254 / 291 ms | 102 / 93 / 54 ms |

Across both runs, the counting pass is 2.1–5.4× faster.

### Goals

- Replace `countPasswordsInDenylistFile`, and the `Files.lines().count()` call in `buildBloomFile`, with a shared byte-scanning `countLines(Path)` helper.
- Return the same count as `BufferedReader.lines().count()` for every terminator style. This includes a `\r\n` pair split across a read-buffer boundary.

### Non-Goals

- Changing the denylist file format, for example adding a header line that holds the count.

### Discussion

_No response_

`DenylistPasswordPolicyProviderFactory.FileBasedPasswordDenylist.loadFromPlaintext` reads a plaintext denylist file twice:

1. `countPasswordsInDenylistFile` counts the lines, which is used to size the `BloomFilter`.
2. A second pass inserts the passwords.

`buildBloomFile`, which backs `kc.sh tools build-password-denylist`, uses the same two passes and counts with `Files.lines().count()`.

The counting pass uses `BufferedReader.lines().count()`. This decodes the entire file as UTF-8 and allocates a `String` for each line, then discards it. The method contains this TODO:

```java
/*
 * TODO find a more efficient way to determine the password count,
 * e.g. require a header-line in the password-denylist file
 */
```

Proposed change: count lines by scanning the raw bytes for `\n` and `\r`. In UTF-8, these byte values never occur inside a multi-byte sequence. A byte scan can therefore produce the same count as `BufferedReader`:

- `\n`, `\r` and `\r\n` are each treated as one line terminator.
- A final line without a terminator is counted.

### Value Proposition

The change reduces the time spent counting lines when a plaintext denylist is loaded, both on first use and on reload (#47163). It also applies to `buildBloomFile`. The file format, configuration and behaviour stay the same.

Measurements were taken on a macOS laptop under moderate background load. Absolute times vary between runs; the ratios were stable.

**Run 1:** [`xato-net-10-million-passwords.txt`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/danielmiessler/SecLists/master/Passwords/Common-Credentials/xato-net-10-million-passwords.txt) (5,189,454 lines, 46 MB, ASCII, `\n` line endings; the same list as in #47356). Three rounds in one JVM.

| | `BufferedReader.lines().count()` | byte scan |
|---|---|---|
| counting pass, cold (first run in a fresh JVM) | 219 ms | 90 ms |
| counting pass within load (3 rounds) | 221 / 181 / 193 ms | 88 / 86 / 61 ms |

**Run 2:** synthetic list of 5,000,000 random passwords (`Pw` + a base-36 random long, 73 MB, `\n` line endings). Three rounds in one JVM.

| | `BufferedReader.lines().count()` | byte scan |
|---|---|---|
| counting pass, warm (best of 5) | 162 ms | 31 ms |
| counting pass, cold (first run in a fresh JVM) | 241 ms | 100 ms |
| counting pass within load (3 rounds) | 247 / 254 / 291 ms | 102 / 93 / 54 ms |

Across both runs, the counting pass is 2.1–5.4× faster.

### Goals

- Replace `countPasswordsInDenylistFile`, and the `Files.lines().count()` call in `buildBloomFile`, with a shared byte-scanning `countLines(Path)` helper.
- Return the same count as `BufferedReader.lines().count()` for every terminator style. This includes a `\r\n` pair split across a read-buffer boundary.

### Non-Goals

- Changing the denylist file format, for example adding a header line that holds the count.

body_text:
### Before reporting an issue

- [x] I have read and understood the issue submission terms, including the current-release reproduction requirement.

### Area

core

### Describe the bug

A forced browser login that starts before the existing SSO session's absolute maximum and completes OTP after that maximum can fail with `ModelIllegalStateException: Session has already aged, concurrent requests to create it should not happen`.

This reproduces on stock Keycloak 26.8.1 (the current release checked today), with persistent user sessions backed by PostgreSQL 16.14, in a single-node disposable container. It also reproduces on 26.7.0. No custom provider or core patch is loaded. The test uses a required OTP browser flow; a brokered Google-compatible local OIDC fixture exhibits the expiry failure too. No AIA cancellation is needed.

### Version

26.8.1 (also reproduced on 26.7.0)

### Regression

Not established.

### Expected behavior

Authentication that crosses the SSO maximum should either establish a valid new login lifetime after the required authentication or return an intentional recoverable authentication error. It should not fail a persistence transaction or return an authorization code that cannot be exchanged.

### Actual behavior

On 26.8.1, the expired-login completion returns a Keycloak error page. The server logs contain:

```
org.keycloak.models.ModelIllegalStateException: Session has already aged, concurrent requests to create it should not happen
    at org.keycloak.models.sessions.infinispan.changes.JpaChangesPerformer.processUserSessionUpdate(JpaChangesPerformer.java:385)
```

On 26.7.0 the password/OTP route produces the same exception (line 398). The broker route can instead return a callback whose code exchange fails with HTTP 400 `invalid_grant` and a server-side `CODE_TO_TOKEN_ERROR` / `invalid_code` event. The exact internal code-note race behind that variant has not been instrumented.

The observed failures grant no application admission. Expired refresh tokens fail. On 26.7.0, starting one new authorization request in the same browser recovered after each route's failure, without clearing cookies, purging database rows, restarting the server, or waiting for background cleanup. The retry performs Google/OTP again. Recovery can retain or change `sid`; applications should not assume either. On 26.8.1, the first fresh Google/OTP authorization request recovered after both the password-route and Google-route error pages. Both retained sid and refreshed successfully. No cookies or rows were cleared in those runs either.

### How to Reproduce?

1. Run stock Keycloak with PostgreSQL-backed persistent online sessions. Enable a confidential OIDC browser client with authorization code + PKCE S256 and a browser flow requiring password and OTP. Configure a user with an existing OTP credential.
2. Before creating the user session, set realm `ssoSessionMaxLifespan=120` and `clientSessionMaxLifespan=120`; leave SSO idle longer than that. Ensure the login/authentication action timeout exceeds 120 seconds. We use 120 seconds to exercise the absolute-boundary case, not to change a session's maximum while it is running.
3. Sign in and obtain the user session's actual `start` timestamp from the admin sessions endpoint.
4. In the same browser, before `start+120s`, begin a new authorization request with `prompt=login` and `max_age=0` (fresh state, nonce and PKCE). Complete the password step, but leave the OTP page open.
5. Wait until after `start+120s`, then submit a valid current OTP.

## Describe the bug

The SSF (Shared Signals Framework) transmitter's synthetic-event emit endpoint (`POST /admin/realms/{realm}/ssf/clients/{receiver}/events/emit`) authorizes callers by reading role claims from the caller's access token rather than checking actual role grants on the user model. This is inconsistent with Keycloak's own admin authorization, where `AdminAuth.hasAppRole`/`hasRealmRole` resolve a `RoleModel` and check `user.hasRole(role) && client.hasScope(role)`.

Because token role claims are shaped by protocol mappers, an attacker with delegated `manage-clients` permission on a single service-account client can add a Hardcoded Role mapper that injects the configured emitter role into the token's `realm_access`/`resource_access` claims. The emit endpoint then accepts the injected claim as proof of authorization, allowing the attacker to emit forged SSF security events (e.g., credential-change, session-revoked, account-disabled) about any subject user and deliver them to the receiver — without any permission on the receiver client itself.

The same claim-based pattern exists in `SsfAuthUtil.checkScopePermission` for the `ssf.requiredRole` check.

Note: The SSF feature is currently experimental/preview and is not available in any released version.

## Version

main @ 999.0.0-SNAPSHOT (commit df42fa2f), JDK 17.

## Expected behavior

The emit endpoint should resolve the configured role to a `RoleModel` and verify the caller's actual role grant against the user model, consistent with `AdminAuth`. A role claim injected by a protocol mapper without a corresponding role grant on the service-account user should not satisfy the authorization check.

## Actual behavior

The emit endpoint reads role claims directly from the access token via `SsfAuthUtil.hasRole(AccessToken, String)`, which only inspects `realm_access`/`resource_access` claims. A Hardcoded Role mapper on any client the attacker controls injects the emitter role into the token, and the endpoint accepts it as valid authorization. The attacker can then emit signed SSF events for arbitrary subjects to the configured receiver.

## Anything else?

- Related upstream tracking issue: https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/49254
- The `HardcodedRole` mapper class has no `validateConfig` restriction, so any configured role string is accepted.
- `SsfAuthUtil.hasRole` splits on the first `.` to determine client-scoped roles, while `KeycloakModelUtils.parseRole` (used by `HardcodedRole`) splits on the last `.` — client IDs containing a dot would be parsed differently by each side.

## Acknowledgement

Thank you to haoyangzhang for reporting this issue. As the SSF feature is experimental/preview and the attack requires delegated admin privileges with manage-clients permission, this is considered a weakness and handled publicly.

### Before reporting an issue

- [x] I have read and understood the above terms for submitting issues, and I understand that my issue may be closed without action if I do not follow them.

### Area

admin/api

### Describe the bug

A newly created realm's built-in `broker` client is bearer-only and has no client secret. Updating only its name and description through Admin REST API v1 generates a secret, although the request contains no credential or authentication changes.

This is the absent-secret counterpart to #48868. The fix in #49714 correctly preserves existing bearer-only credentials, but removing the bearer-only branch also causes `determineNewSecret` to generate a credential when both the stored and requested secret are null. Preserving an absent credential should not undo support for existing secrets or change new-client generation.

### Version

26.8.1; the same generation branch remains in main at a33d89187e6e6cd41a1211cebd26f243d4fd3c9a

### Regression

- [x] The issue is a regression

Source comparison identifies #49714 as the behavior change: its predecessor returned null for bearer-only clients. Actual HTTP reproduction was performed on the latest stable 26.8.1, rather than an older binary.

### Expected behavior

A metadata-only update of an existing client that remains bearer-only preserves the absence of its credential. Existing bearer-only secrets, explicit secret changes, new-client secret generation and access-type transitions retain their current behavior.

### Actual behavior

The built-in broker starts with no secret. After a name/description-only PUT, it has a generated secret. No credential was supplied in the update.

### How to Reproduce?

Use a disposable, freshly initialized 26.8.1 instance and an authenticated administrator. Set `KC_URL` and `ADMIN_TOKEN` for that local instance. The commands below print credential presence only:

```sh
BROKER_ID=$(curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  "$KC_URL/admin/realms/master/clients?clientId=broker" | jq -r '.[0].id')

curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  "$KC_URL/admin/realms/master/clients/$BROKER_ID" \
  | jq '{clientId, bearerOnly, hasSecret: (.secret != null)}'
# hasSecret: false

curl -fsS -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Updated broker","description":"Metadata only"}' \
  "$KC_URL/admin/realms/master/clients/$BROKER_ID"

curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  "$KC_URL/admin/realms/master/clients/$BROKER_ID" \
  | jq '{clientId, bearerOnly, hasSecret: (.secret != null)}'
# Actual: hasSecret: true; expected: false
```

### Anything else?

The related merged change is #49714, closing #48868; this report concerns preserving a missing credential rather than preserving a present one.

A small local patch captures whether the client was already non-public/bearer-only before applying fields, and preserves null only when that client remains bearer-only and no secret is supplied. A release-matched rebuilt 26.8.1 SPI JAR in a disposable official 26.8.1 container preserves null for the metadata PUT while seven creation/retention/replacement/transition checks keep passing. The current-main SPI modules also compile.

A separate local Terraform check used an existing provider build based on 5.10.0 with bearer-only/read-suppression support. Import, suppression adoption and metadata repair converge while the broker credential remains null. The initial importer makes three secret GETs, all returning no value; no secret POST occurs and no credential value enters plan/state.

Six regression methods were added locally to the existing native `ClientTest`. They have not yet been compiled or run in its integration harness: that requires an 82-module prerequisite build. The local HTTP/Terraform proof is a release-matched 26.8.1 run, not a current-main server integration run.

AI assistance: Codex agents assisted with investigation, implementation, regression-test preparation and local validation.

body_text:
### Description

The Aurora cleanup script at `.github/scripts/aws/rds/aurora_delete.sh` can report success while leaving an Aurora DB cluster and its VPC behind.

The current flow requests deletion of all DB instances, immediately calls `delete-db-cluster`, and only then waits for the instances. AWS rejects cluster deletion while it still contains instances that are not in a deleting/deleted state. That error is suppressed with `|| true`, and cluster deletion is never retried after the instances disappear.

The final VPC retry loop also returns success after exhausting all attempts, even when the VPC was not deleted.

This can leave billable Aurora clusters and VPCs after completed or cancelled CI runs.

### Required cleanup changes

- Discover the target DB cluster and tagged VPC idempotently.
- Capture DB cluster members once before starting deletion.
- Delete reader instances before the writer to avoid unnecessary failover.
- Wait for all DB instances to be deleted.
- Delete the DB cluster only after its instances are gone.
- Wait for DB cluster deletion before removing subnet groups, subnets, security groups, the internet gateway, route tables, and the VPC.
- Treat an already absent DB cluster or VPC as successful cleanup.
- Do not suppress unexpected AWS authorization or API failures.
- Fail the script if VPC deletion still fails after all retries.
- Validate that the Aurora tag resolves to exactly one VPC rather than passing an empty or multi-value identifier to AWS commands.

### Use one isolated test VPC for EC2 and Aurora

Aurora does not itself need public internet access. It is currently public because the EC2 test instance is implicitly created in the account's default VPC, while Aurora is created in a separate dedicated VPC. The EC2 instance therefore reaches Aurora through its public endpoint.

Change the test topology to one dedicated VPC owned by the CI run:

- Create one public subnet for the EC2 test instance.
- Create private Aurora subnets in at least two availability zones and use only those subnets in the DB subnet group.
- Attach an internet gateway and add the default route only to the EC2 public subnet's route table. The gateway remains necessary because the GitHub-hosted runner connects to EC2 over its public IP using SSH.
- Explicitly create the EC2 security group and EC2 instance in this VPC/public subnet instead of relying on the account's default VPC.
- Keep a public IP on EC2 for the existing SSH-based Ansible flow.
- Create Aurora instances with `--no-publicly-accessible`.
- Allow PostgreSQL ingress to the Aurora security group only from the EC2 security group; remove ingress from `0.0.0.0/0`.
- Pass or expose the VPC id, EC2 subnet id, and Aurora security-group id between the Aurora action, workflow, and EC2 Ansible role as needed.
- Keep all networking tagged with the Aurora cluster/run identifier so the asynchronous cleanup workflow owns and can remove the complete test environment.
- Preserve cleanup ordering: delete EC2 and its security group before deleting the Aurora networking. Cleanup must also handle partially created environments.

This retains CI-run isolation, keeps the existing GitHub-runner-to-EC2 SSH mechanism, and removes public database exposure. It does not eliminate the internet gateway, because EC2 still needs it; it limits the gateway route to the public EC2 subnet.

### Additional creation-side follow-ups

- In `aurora_create.sh`, avoid the broad `starts_with(DBInstanceIdentifier, AURORA_CLUSTER)` collision check; check the DB cluster identifier or the full instance-name prefix.
- Clean up partially created networking when database or EC2 creation fails.

### Acceptance criteria

Add automated tests or mocked AWS CLI coverage for:

- A cluster with reader and writer instances.
- An already absent cluster with leftover networking.
- No matching resources.
- AWS authorization/API failure.
- VPC dependencies that remain after all retries.
- Duplicate VPCs with the same `AuroraCluster` tag.
- EC2 being created in the run-specific VPC and public subnet.
- Aurora instances being private and placed only in the private DB subnets.
- The Aurora security group accepting port 5432 from the EC2 security group, with no `0.0.0.0/0` database ingress.
- Only the EC2 public subnet having a default route through the internet gateway.
- Successful teardown of EC2, Aurora, the internet gateway, route tables, subnets, security groups, and the VPC.

The equivalent cleanup flow in `keycloak-benchmark` has exposed the same failure mode and is being hardened there.

{"repository": "keycloak/keycloak", "task_candidate_id": 9451, "repository_id": 143, "issue_number": 54077, "github_issue_id": 5898183269, "html_url": "https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/54077", "created_at": "2026-10-17T12:10:21+00:00", "author_association": "MEMBER", "title": "Harden Aurora CI cleanup to avoid leaking DB clusters and VPCs", "body_text": "### Description

The Aurora cleanup script at `.github/scripts/aws/rds/aurora_delete.sh` can report success while leaving an Aurora DB cluster and its VPC behind.

The current flow requests deletion of all DB instances, immediately calls `delete-db-cluster`, and only then waits for the instances. AWS rejects cluster deletion while it still contains instances that are not in a deleting/deleted state. That error is suppressed with `|| true`, and cluster deletion is never retried after the instances disappear.

The final VPC retry loop also returns success after exhausting all attempts, even when the VPC was not deleted.

This can leave billable Aurora clusters and VPCs after completed or cancelled CI runs.

### Required cleanup changes

- Discover the target DB cluster and tagged VPC idempotently.
- Capture DB cluster members once before starting deletion.
- Delete reader instances before the writer to avoid unnecessary failover.
- Wait for all DB instances to be deleted.
- Delete the DB cluster only after its instances are gone.
- Wait for DB cluster deletion before removing subnet groups, subnets, security groups, the internet gateway, route tables, and the VPC.
- Treat an already absent DB cluster or VPC as successful cleanup.
- Do not suppress unexpected AWS authorization or API failures.
- Fail the script if VPC deletion still fails after all retries.
- Validate that the Aurora tag resolves to exactly one VPC rather than passing an empty or multi-value identifier to AWS commands.

### Use one isolated test VPC for EC2 and Aurora

Aurora does not itself need public internet access. It is currently public because the EC2 test instance is implicitly created in the account's default VPC, while Aurora is created in a separate dedicated VPC. The EC2 instance therefore reaches Aurora through its public endpoint.

Change the test topology to one dedicated VPC owned by the CI run:

- Create one public subnet for the EC2 test instance.
- Create private Aurora subnets in at least two availability zones and use only those subnets in the DB subnet group.
- Attach an internet gateway and add the default route only to the EC2 public subnet's route table. The gateway remains necessary because the GitHub-hosted runner connects to EC2 over its public IP using SSH.
- Explicitly create the EC2 security group and EC2 instance in this VPC/public subnet instead of relying on the account's default VPC.
- Keep a public IP on EC2 for the existing SSH-based Ansible flow.
- Create Aurora instances with `--no-publicly-accessible`.
- Allow PostgreSQL ingress to the Aurora security group only from the EC2 security group; remove ingress from `0.0.0.0/0`.
- Pass or expose the VPC id, EC2 subnet id, and Aurora security-group id between the Aurora action, workflow, and EC2 Ansible role as needed.
- Keep all networking tagged with the Aurora cluster/run identifier so the asynchronous cleanup workflow owns and can remove the complete test environment.
- Preserve cleanup ordering: delete EC2 and its security group before deleting the Aurora networking. Cleanup must also handle partially created environments.

This retains CI-run isolation, keeps the existing GitHub-runner-to-EC2 SSH mechanism, and removes public database exposure. It does not eliminate the internet gateway, because EC2 still needs it; it limits the gateway route to the public EC2 subnet.

### Additional creation-side follow-ups

- In `aurora_create.sh`, avoid the broad `starts_with(DBInstanceIdentifier, AURORA_CLUSTER)` collision check; check the DB cluster identifier or the full instance-name prefix.
- Clean up partially created networking when database or EC2 creation fails.

### Acceptance criteria

Add automated tests or mocked AWS CLI coverage for:

- A cluster with reader and writer instances.
- An already absent cluster with leftover networking.
- No matching resources.
- AWS authorization/API failure.
- VPC dependencies that remain after all retries.
- Duplicate VPCs with the same `AuroraCluster` tag.
- EC2 being created in the run-specific VPC and public subnet.
- Aurora instances being private and placed only in the private DB subnets.
- The Aurora security group accepting port 5432 from the EC2 security group, with no `0.0.0.0/0` database ingress.
- Only the EC2 public subnet having a default route through the internet gateway.
- Successful teardown of EC2, Aurora, the internet gateway, route tables, subnets, security groups, and the VPC.

The equivalent cleanup flow in `keycloak-benchmark` has exposed the same failure mode and is being hardened there.

### Description

Today, when a verifiable credential is issued through the OID4VCI issuance flow, a record is created in the issued credentials storage at the time the token is requested. This record exists even if the holder never completes the flow and never actually receives the credential. As a result, anyone looking at the list of issued credentials for a user has no way to know which credentials were truly delivered and which ones are just remnants of an abandoned or failed issuance attempt.

This causes real problems. An administrator reviewing a user's issued credentials cannot trust the list. Integration systems that read the issued credentials endpoint may incorrectly assume every listed credential was successfully handed to its holder. And a user's credential history can accumulate stale, misleading entries with no distinguishing information.

The solution is to add an explicit completion marker. When the issuance flow reaches the point where the credential has been successfully delivered to the holder, the system marks that issued credential record as completed. Records from attempts that never reached delivery stay unmarked.

With this change, any consumer of the issued credentials list can reliably distinguish a credential that was truly delivered from one that was only prepared but never handed over. Existing records are treated as not completed, since there is no evidence they were delivered, and the flag is set only at the moment of confirmed delivery.

### Before reporting an issue

- [x] I have read and understood the above terms for submitting issues, and I understand that my issue may be closed without action if I do not follow them.

### Area

account/api

### Describe the bug

Keycloak 26.8.0 is running behind an HTTPS reverse proxy with separate hostnames for public OIDC endpoints and the Admin Console.

**Environment:**
- Keycloak: 26.8.0
- OS: Windows Server 2025
- Java: OpenJDK 25.0.2
- Database: Microsoft SQL Server Express 2022 (TLS)
- Reverse proxy: OpenText Access Manager (Access Gateway)
- Deployment: Single Keycloak instance running as a Windows Service
- TLS: HTTPS on port 443 externally, re-encrypted to Keycloak on port 8443

**Relevant `keycloak.conf` configuration:**

```properties
hostname=https://example.com
hostname-admin=https://example-admin.com
hostname-strict=true

http-enabled=false
https-port=8443
proxy-headers=xforwarded
```

With `proxy-headers=xforwarded`, Keycloak correctly logs the real client IP addresses. However, saving changes in the web-based Admin Console fails with **HTTP 403 Forbidden**.

The Admin Console displays:

**Realm could not be updated: Invalid origin**

The reverse proxy sends the following headers, which were also verified using Keycloak's `hostname-debug` endpoint:

```http
X-Forwarded-For: 192.0.2.10
X-Forwarded-Host: example-admin.com
X-Forwarded-Proto: https
X-Forwarded-Port: 443
```

The server-side DEBUG log reveals an origin mismatch involving the backend port `8443`, even though the browser accesses the Admin Console on the standard HTTPS port `443`.

Switching to `proxy-headers=forwarded` resolves the administrative errors, but Keycloak then logs the reverse proxy IP instead of the actual client IP.

### Version

26.8.0

### Regression

- [ ] The issue is a regression

### Expected behavior

With `X-Forwarded-Port: 443`, Keycloak should correctly validate the request against the external origin `https://example-admin.com`, without using the internal backend port `8443`.

Saving changes in the Admin Console should succeed without an `Invalid origin` error.

According to the Keycloak documentation, `X-Forwarded-Port` takes precedence over the port in `X-Forwarded-Host`.

### Actual behavior

When saving realm settings in the Admin Console, the following error is displayed:

**Realm could not be updated: Invalid origin**

The corresponding Admin REST API request returns **HTTP 403 Forbidden**:

```http
PUT https://example-admin.com/admin/realms/test-realm/ui-ext
Origin: https://example-admin.com
Host: example-admin.com
```

The Keycloak DEBUG log shows:

```text
Invalid CORS request: origin https://example-admin.com:8443 not in allowed origins [https://example-admin.com]
```

Keycloak appears to use the internal backend port `8443` during origin validation instead of the forwarded external port `443`.

### How to Reproduce?

1. Configure Keycloak 26.8.0 behind an HTTPS reverse proxy with external port `443` and backend port `8443`.
2. Configure separate `hostname` and `hostname-admin` values, as shown above.
3. Set `proxy-headers=xforwarded`.
4. Configure the reverse proxy to forward `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Forwarded-Host`, `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`, and `X-Forwarded-Port: 443`.
5. Log in to the Admin Console at `https://example-admin.com/admin/test-realm/console/`.
6. Open Realm Settings, modify a setting, and click Save.
7. Observe HTTP 403 Forbidden and the error **Realm could not be updated: Invalid origin**.

The server-side DEBUG log reports an origin mismatch involving port `8443`.

### Anything else?

**Server-side DEBUG log:**

```text
2026-10-16 16:13:34,358 DEBUG [org.keycloak.services.cors.DefaultCors] (executor-thread-12) Invalid CORS request: origin https://example-admin.com:8443 not in allowed origins [https://example-admin.com]

2026-10-16 16:13:34,358 DEBUG [org.keycloak.services.error.KeycloakErrorHandler] (executor-thread-12) Error response Forbidden: jakarta.ws.rs.ForbiddenException: Invalid origin

    at org.keycloak.services.cors.DefaultCors.checkOrigin(DefaultCors.java:215)

    at org.keycloak.services.cors.DefaultCors.checkAllowedOrigins(DefaultCors.java:95)

    at org.keycloak.services.cors.DefaultCors.checkAllowedOrigins(DefaultCors.java:106)

    at org.keycloak.services.resources.admin.AdminRoot.getRealmsAdmin(AdminRoot.java:259)

    at org.keycloak.services.resources.admin.AdminRoot$quarkusrestinvoker$getRealmsAdmin_e9e564a2c5fdea05832c9c2326104217661e6d1c.invoke(Unknown Source)

    at org.jboss.resteasy.reactive.server.handlers.InvocationHandler.handle(InvocationHandler.java:29)

    at org.keycloak.quarkus.runtime.integration.resteasy.TransactionalSessionHandler.handle(TransactionalSessionHandler.java:85)

    at io.quarkus.resteasy.reactive.server.runtime.QuarkusResteasyReactiveRequestContext.invokeHandler(QuarkusResteasyReactiveRequestContext.java:195)

    at org.jboss.resteasy.reactive.common.core.AbstractResteasyReactiveContext.run(AbstractResteasyReactiveContext.java:150)

    at io.quarkus.vertx.core.runtime.VertxCoreRecorder$15.runWith(VertxCoreRecorder.java:695)

    at org.jboss.threads.EnhancedQueueExecutor$Task.doRunWith(EnhancedQueueExecutor.java:2651)

    at org.jboss.threads.EnhancedQueueExecutor$Task.run(EnhancedQueueExecutor.java:2630)

    at org.jboss.threads.EnhancedQueueExecutor.runThreadBody(EnhancedQueueExecutor.java:1622)

    at org.jboss.threads.EnhancedQueueExecutor$ThreadBody.run(EnhancedQueueExecutor.java:1589)

    at org.jboss.threads.DelegatingRunnable.run(DelegatingRunnable.java:11)

    at org.jboss.threads.ThreadLocalResettingRunnable.run(ThreadLocalResettingRunnable.java:11)

    at io.netty.util.concurrent.FastThreadLocalRunnable.run(FastThreadLocalRunnable.java:30)

    at java.base/java.lang.Thread.run(Thread.java:1474)
```

**Workaround – working configuration**

We discovered that **changing the load balancer to send `X-Forwarded-Port: 8443` instead of `443` resolves the issue**.

Working headers:

```http
X-Forwarded-For: 192.0.2.10
X-Forwarded-Host: example-admin.com
X-Forwarded-Proto: https
X-Forwarded-Port: 8443
```

With this configuration:

- Admin Console operations, including saving realm settings, work successfully.
- The `Invalid origin` error disappears.
- Keycloak correctly logs the actual client IP addresses.
- OIDC discovery endpoints advertise the correct public URLs without the internal port `8443`.

Everything we tested now works as expected.

However, using `8443` in `X-Forwarded-Port` seems counterintuitive because clients connect to the reverse proxy on port `443`.

**Is this expected behavior in Keycloak 26.8.0, or could this indicate an issue with origin validation when using `hostname-admin`, `proxy-headers=xforwarded`, and HTTPS re-encryption on a different backend port?**

### Area

account/api

### Describe the bug

Keycloak 26.8.0 is running behind an HTTPS reverse proxy with separate hostnames for public OIDC endpoints and the Admin Console.

**Environment:**
- Keycloak: 26.8.0
- OS: Windows Server 2025
- Java: OpenJDK 25.0.2
- Database: Microsoft SQL Server Express 2022 (TLS)
- Reverse proxy: OpenText Access Manager (Access Gateway)
- Deployment: Single Keycloak instance running as a Windows Service
- TLS: HTTPS on port 443 externally, re-encrypted to Keycloak on port 8443

**Relevant `keycloak.conf` configuration:**

```properties
hostname=https://example.com
hostname-admin=https://example-admin.com
hostname-strict=true

http-enabled=false
https-port=8443
proxy-headers=xforwarded
```

With `proxy-headers=xforwarded`, Keycloak correctly logs the real client IP addresses. However, saving changes in the web-based Admin Console fails with **HTTP 403 Forbidden**.

The Admin Console displays:

**Realm could not be updated: Invalid origin**

The reverse proxy sends the following headers, which were also verified using Keycloak's `hostname-debug` endpoint:

```http
X-Forwarded-For: 192.0.2.10
X-Forwarded-Host: example-admin.com
X-Forwarded-Proto: https
X-Forwarded-Port: 443
```

The server-side DEBUG log reveals an origin mismatch involving the backend port `8443`, even though the browser accesses the Admin Console on the standard HTTPS port `443`.

Switching to `proxy-headers=forwarded` resolves the administrative errors, but Keycloak then logs the reverse proxy IP instead of the actual client IP.

### Version

26.8.0

### Regression

- [ ] The issue is a regression

### Expected behavior

With `X-Forwarded-Port: 443`, Keycloak should correctly validate the request against the external origin `https://example-admin.com`, without using the internal backend port `8443`.

Saving changes in the Admin Console should succeed without an `Invalid origin` error.

According to the Keycloak documentation, `X-Forwarded-Port` takes precedence over the port in `X-Forwarded-Host`.

### Actual behavior

When saving realm settings in the Admin Console, the following error is displayed:

**Realm could not be updated: Invalid origin**

The corresponding Admin REST API request returns **HTTP 403 Forbidden**:

```http
PUT https://example-admin.com/admin/realms/test-realm/ui-ext
Origin: https://example-admin.com
Host: example-admin.com
```

The Keycloak DEBUG log shows:

```text
Invalid CORS request: origin https://example-admin.com:8443 not in allowed origins [https://example-admin.com]
```

Keycloak appears to use the internal backend port `8443` during origin validation instead of the forwarded external port `443`.

### How to Reproduce?

1. Configure Keycloak 26.8.0 behind an HTTPS reverse proxy with external port `443` and backend port `8443`.
2. Configure separate `hostname` and `hostname-admin` values, as shown above.
3. Set `proxy-headers=xforwarded`.
4. Configure the reverse proxy to forward `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Forwarded-Host`, `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`, and `X-Forwarded-Port: 443`.
5. Log in to the Admin Console at `https://example-admin.com/admin/test-realm/console/`.
6. Open Realm Settings, modify a setting, and click Save.
7. Observe HTTP 403 Forbidden and the error **Realm could not be updated: Invalid origin**.

The server-side DEBUG log reports an origin mismatch involving port `8443`.

### Anything else?

**Server-side DEBUG log:**

```text

    at org.jboss.resteasy.reactive.server.handlers.InvocationHandler.handle(InvocationHandler.java:29)

    at org.keycloak.quarkus.runtime.integration.resteasy.TransactionalSessionHandler.handle(TransactionalSessionHandler.java:85)

    at io.quarkus.resteasy.reactive.server.runtime.QuarkusResteasyReactiveRequestContext.invokeHandler(QuarkusResteasyReactiveRequestContext.java:195)

    at org.jboss.resteasy.reactive.common.core.AbstractResteasyReactiveContext.run(AbstractResteasyReactiveContext.java:150)

    at io.quarkus.vertx.core.runtime.VertxCoreRecorder$15.runWith(VertxCoreRecorder.java:695)

    at org.jboss.threads.EnhancedQueueExecutor$Task.doRunWith(EnhancedQueueExecutor.java:2651)

    at org.jboss.threads.EnhancedQueueExecutor$Task.run(EnhancedQueueExecutor.java:2630)

    at java.base/java.lang.Thread.run(Thread.java:1474)
```

**Workaround – working configuration**

We discovered that **changing the load balancer to send `X-Forwarded-Port: 8443` instead of `443` resolves the issue**.

Working headers:

```http
X-Forwarded-For: 192.0.2.10
X-Forwarded-Host: example-admin.com
X-Forwarded-Proto: https
X-Forwarded-Port: 8443
```

With this configuration:

- Admin Console operations, including saving realm settings, work successfully.
- The `Invalid origin` error disappears.
- Keycloak correctly logs the actual client IP addresses.
- OIDC discovery endpoints advertise the correct public URLs without the internal port `8443`.

Everything we tested now works as expected.

However, using `8443` in `X-Forwarded-Port` seems counterintuitive because clients connect to the reverse proxy on port `443`.

### Description

Organization Identity-First Login does not redirect a user who has a first-factor credential: `OrganizationAuthenticator.tryRedirectBroker` returns early, so the user gets the password form. In a migration where users still hold passwords from before their organization moved to an external identity provider, those users are never sent to that provider. Removing their credentials is not always an option, and some accounts (break-glass, service desk) must keep the local login.

The domain matched against organization domains is always taken from the e-mail address. Directories that identify users by another attribute (a UPN that differs from the e-mail, for example) cannot route by it.

### Value Proposition

Lets a realm move an organization to its own identity provider without first deleting every local credential, while keeping named accounts on the local form, and supports directories where the routing domain is not the e-mail domain.

### Goals

- An option to redirect users that have local credentials too, to the broker the organization's domain routes to (or the one that provisioned a managed member).
- A list of users that are never redirected while that option is on.
- An option naming the user attribute the domain is taken from; the e-mail address when unset.

### Non-Goals

- Changing the default behaviour.
- Mapping domains to identity providers outside an organization.

### Discussion

_No response_

### Notes

All three are configuration of the existing `organization` authenticator.

### Area

oid4vc

### Describe the bug

The Admin UI treats the relevant realm attribute as a boolean while the backend expects a comma-separated list of algorithms.

Compare

https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/blob/6d2c039b9abcf01eb94de588b6233a4aaa7c2387/js/apps/admin-ui/src/realm-settings/TokensTab.tsx#L748-L758

with 

https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/blob/e0756392d1e19be1db4dc11872b15da4990f2345/services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/protocol/oid4vc/issuance/OID4VCIssuerWellKnownProvider.java#L453-L465

This misaligned treatment affects the validity of the issuer metadata, which advertise a non-compliant empty array under "zip_values_supported".

### Version

26.8

### Regression

- [ ] The issue is a regression

### Expected behavior

The treatment must be consistent. The natural option: Configuration on the Admin UI should either set "DEF" or null.

### Actual behavior

Configuration on the Admin UI currently sets "true" or "false", which is not understood by the backend.

### How to Reproduce?

- Start Keycloak with OID4VCI features.
- Update some value under Realm Settings > Tokens > OID4VCI Attributes, then save the form.
- Export realm attributes and notice that `oid4vci.request.zip.algorithms` is set to `false`.

### Anything else?

_No response_

### Description

The OIDC **Organization Group Membership** mapper supports adding roles inherited from organization groups through `addGroupRoleMappings`. However, it always emits the `groups` claim. There is no independent option to include group-derived roles while omitting group names and paths.

Add an independent option, such as **Include group membership**, so applications can receive organization-scoped roles without the underlying group membership paths.

### Value Proposition

Applications using role-based authorization may need organization-scoped roles without needing the underlying group structure. Including every group membership adds unnecessary token size, especially for users belonging to many groups or groups with long paths.

Disabling the mapper also removes its organization-scoped role output, so the existing token inclusion switches do not address this use case.

### Goals

- Add an independent option to include or omit organization-group membership paths.
- Default the option to `true` to preserve existing behavior.
- When disabled, omit the `groups` property entirely, including an empty array.
- Continue emitting organization-scoped roles when `addGroupRoleMappings=true`.
- Preserve existing organization selection, composite-role expansion, and token inclusion settings.

For example, with group membership disabled and role mappings enabled, the desired claim would be:

```json
{
  "organization": {
    "acme": {
      "id": "<organization-id>",
      "resource_access": {
        "example-api": {
          "roles": ["editor"]
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

The user would still belong to organization groups in Keycloak and inherit their roles; only the group membership paths would be omitted from the token.

### Non-Goals

- Selective group filtering or group allowlists.
- Changes to group membership, role assignment, or authorization semantics.
- Changes to existing top-level role claims.

### Notes

The mapper currently writes `groups` unconditionally, while `addGroupRoleMappings` controls only whether role claims are added. This request concerns independent control over group membership and role output.

- [OrganizationGroupMembershipMapper implementation (26.8.1)](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/blob/26.8.1/services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/organization/protocol/mappers/oidc/OrganizationGroupMembershipMapper.java)
- [Original organization-group mapper issue #45511](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/45511)

### Description

Keycloak verifies WebAuthn attestation statements against certificates imported into the truststore and can restrict authenticators with a static AAGUID allow-list, but it has no access to the metadata the FIDO Alliance publishes for authenticator models. 
This enhancement adds a `webauthn-metadata` SPI with a FIDO Metadata Service (MDS) provider, uses the attestation root certificates from the metadata as trust anchors, and adds two policy options based on the metadata:  

a minimum **Authenticator certification** level and **Acceptable key protection types**.

### Value Proposition

Administrators can express requirements in terms the FIDO ecosystem already defines, such as "FIDO Certified Level 2 or higher" or "key protected by a secure element", instead of maintaining AAGUID lists by hand. Revoked or compromised authenticator models are rejected automatically. The metadata also supplies the attestation roots needed to verify AAGUIDs, which removes the need to import vendor root certificates into the truststore one by one, and provides display names for authenticator models missing from the built-in list.

### Goals

- `webauthn-metadata` SPI (`org.keycloak.webauthn.metadata`) with a `fido-mds` provider: remote MDS3 BLOB (`blob-url`) with signature and certificate chain verification against the MDS root (GlobalSign Root CA - R3 bundled, `root-certificate` overridable, optional CRL `revocation-check`), or a local BLOB file (`blob-file`, relative paths resolved against `conf/`) for environments without internet access. Background prefetch, refresh after the BLOB's `nextUpdate`, last good BLOB kept on failure with a retry backoff. Lookups by AAGUID and, for U2F, by attestation certificate key identifier.
- Attestation roots from the metadata merged with the truststore anchors in the attestation chain verification.
- Policy options on both WebAuthn policies: `authenticatorCertification` (`not specified`, `listed`, `FIDO_CERTIFIED`, `FIDO_CERTIFIED_L1` … `FIDO_CERTIFIED_L3plus`) and `acceptableKeyProtectionTypes` (`software`, `hardware`, `tee`, `secure_element`, `remote_handle`, `sync_fabric`). Both require an attestation format other than `none` and disable self attestation; `REVOKED` and the compromise statuses reject the model regardless of level.
- Credential display name falls back to the metadata description when the AAGUID is not in the built-in passkey metadata file.
- Admin console, documentation, unit and integration tests.

### Non-Goals

- A native, browser-free authentication API for mobile apps.
- Enforcing the metadata status at authentication time; the metadata is consulted at registration only.
- Replacing the built-in AAGUID display-name file with MDS data; MDS only complements it.
- Automatic activation. The provider stays inactive until a BLOB URL or file is configured.

### Discussion

Related: #46400

### Notes

- Additional `webauthn4j-metadata` library with the same version as the existing `webauthn4j-core`, needs to be added to the distribution. It pulls `jackson-datatype-jsr310`, which Quarkus already provides.
- The webauthn4j-metadata can download a file (blob.jwt) from the fido metadata service (MDS: https://fidoalliance.org/metadata/) or work with a fixed configured local file. The blob.jwt file contains the known devices with their AAGUIDs and a classification.
- Suggested testing approach: Chrome's virtual authenticator signs attestations with a fixed, public key and subject, so a self-signed certificate for that key works as MDS trust anchor in a generated test BLOB (`WebAuthnMetadataPolicyTest`, `FidoMdsServerConfig`). Unit tests cover the policy verifier, the store (indexing, backoff, stale serving) and the factory (file resolution, root certificate loading).

Keycloak verifies WebAuthn attestation statements against certificates imported into the truststore and can restrict authenticators with a static AAGUID allow-list, but it has no access to the metadata the FIDO Alliance publishes for authenticator models. 
This enhancement adds a `webauthn-metadata` SPI with a FIDO Metadata Service (MDS) provider, uses the attestation root certificates from the metadata as trust anchors, and adds two policy options based on the metadata:  

a minimum **Authenticator certification** level and **Acceptable key protection types**.

### Value Proposition

Administrators can express requirements in terms the FIDO ecosystem already defines, such as "FIDO Certified Level 2 or higher" or "key protected by a secure element", instead of maintaining AAGUID lists by hand. Revoked or compromised authenticator models are rejected automatically. The metadata also supplies the attestation roots needed to verify AAGUIDs, which removes the need to import vendor root certificates into the truststore one by one, and provides display names for authenticator models missing from the built-in list.

### Goals

- `webauthn-metadata` SPI (`org.keycloak.webauthn.metadata`) with a `fido-mds` provider: remote MDS3 BLOB (`blob-url`) with signature and certificate chain verification against the MDS root (GlobalSign Root CA - R3 bundled, `root-certificate` overridable, optional CRL `revocation-check`), or a local BLOB file (`blob-file`, relative paths resolved against `conf/`) for environments without internet access. Background prefetch, refresh after the BLOB's `nextUpdate`, last good BLOB kept on failure with a retry backoff. Lookups by AAGUID and, for U2F, by attestation certificate key identifier.
- Attestation roots from the metadata merged with the truststore anchors in the attestation chain verification.
- Policy options on both WebAuthn policies: `authenticatorCertification` (`not specified`, `listed`, `FIDO_CERTIFIED`, `FIDO_CERTIFIED_L1` … `FIDO_CERTIFIED_L3plus`) and `acceptableKeyProtectionTypes` (`software`, `hardware`, `tee`, `secure_element`, `remote_handle`, `sync_fabric`). Both require an attestation format other than `none` and disable self attestation; `REVOKED` and the compromise statuses reject the model regardless of level.
- Credential display name falls back to the metadata description when the AAGUID is not in the built-in passkey metadata file.
- Admin console, documentation, unit and integration tests.

### Non-Goals

- A native, browser-free authentication API for mobile apps.
- Enforcing the metadata status at authentication time; the metadata is consulted at registration only.
- Replacing the built-in AAGUID display-name file with MDS data; MDS only complements it.
- Automatic activation. The provider stays inactive until a BLOB URL or file is configured.

### Discussion

Related: #46400

### Notes

- Additional `webauthn4j-metadata` library with the same version as the existing `webauthn4j-core`, needs to be added to the distribution. It pulls `jackson-datatype-jsr310`, which Quarkus already provides.
- The webauthn4j-metadata can download a file (blob.jwt) from the fido metadata service (MDS: https://fidoalliance.org/metadata/) or work with a fixed configured local file. The blob.jwt file contains the known devices with their AAGUIDs and a classification.
- Suggested testing approach: Chrome's virtual authenticator signs attestations with a fixed, public key and subject, so a self-signed certificate for that key works as MDS trust anchor in a generated test BLOB (`WebAuthnMetadataPolicyTest`, `FidoMdsServerConfig`). ### Description

`@InjectWebDriver` does not currently let an individual test provide Chrome command-line arguments. Tests that exercise browser features behind flags must therefore modify global browser configuration or create and manage their own WebDriver, bypassing the test framework lifecycle.

This gap was encountered while adding Device Bound Session Credentials coverage, which needs to enable Chrome features for specific browser tests without affecting unrelated tests.

### Value Proposition

Supporting per-test Chrome arguments keeps browser setup inside the test framework, allows tests to opt into experimental or test-only browser features, and avoids leaking configuration across the wider browser suite.

### Goals

- Add a `chromeArguments` attribute to `@InjectWebDriver`.
- Pass those arguments to both Chrome and Chrome Headless sessions.
- Keep drivers requested with different argument sets from being shared as compatible resources.
- Ignore Chrome-specific arguments for other browser implementations.
- Document the option and cover both option construction and a real Chrome session.

### Non-Goals

- Providing a generic Selenium capabilities API.
- Adding browser-specific argument support for Firefox or HtmlUnit.
- Changing the default arguments applied to every Chrome session.
- Enabling any particular experimental browser feature by default.

### Discussion

https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/42257

### Notes

A proposed API shape is:

```java
@InjectWebDriver(chromeArguments = "--enable-features=DeviceBoundSessions")
ManagedWebDriver driver;
```

The implementation should apply the annotation arguments after the framework defaults so explicitly requested test arguments take precedence.

### Description

Promote the `declarative-ui` feature from experimental to supported (enabled by default).

The Declarative UI SPI (`UiPageProvider` / `UiTabProvider`) lets extensions add Admin Console pages and tabs by describing forms with `ProviderConfigProperty`, without a custom React theme.

### Value Proposition

Extensions can ship Admin Console UI for custom providers without maintaining a forked Admin Console theme. Graduating the feature removes the need for `--features=declarative-ui` and provides production support guarantees.

### Goals

- Change `DECLARATIVE_UI` from `Type.EXPERIMENTAL` to `Type.DEFAULT`
- Document the SPI in the UI Customization guide
- Record the promotion in release notes and the upgrading guide
- Remove experimental enablement requirements from examples where appropriate

### Non-Goals

- Closing or resolving open enhancement requests that extend the SPI further (for example custom save types or script-based extensions)
- Changing the SPI APIs themselves in this promotion

### Discussion

https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/discussions/24805

### Notes

Per `docs/features.md`, graduating to supported requires feature completeness for the MVP, documentation without experimental notices, and resolution of blocking feedback. Existing documentation lived primarily in the keycloak-quickstarts `extend-admin-console-spi` example.

### Before reporting an issue

- [x] I have read and understood the above terms for submitting issues, and I understand that my issue may be closed without action if I do not follow them.

### Area

authentication

### Describe the bug

A client policy with the condition `client-attributes` is not applied on the `REGISTER` event: a client created with
the matching attribute passes the policy's executors. The first update of the same client, even unchanged, is checked
and rejected. So a client that violates the policy can be created and then keeps working (until someone saves it).

`ClientAttributesCondition.applyPolicy` only looks at `PRE_AUTHORIZATION_REQUEST` and at a `ClientModelContext`;
when the client is created there is no populated client model yet, so the condition votes `NO` instead of evaluating
the attributes of the proposed `ClientRepresentation`. Related, same cause for workflows: #51594 (the client is not
populated yet when its creation event fires).

### Version

26.8.1 (also 26.8.0)

### Regression

- [ ] The issue is a regression

### Expected behavior

creating a client whose attributes match the condition runs the policy's executors, as the
conditions `any-client` or `client-access-type` do - here: the client with an insecure redirect URI is rejected
(HTTP 400 "Invalid Redirect Uri").

### Actual behavior

the client is created (HTTP 201). Saving it unchanged right afterwards fails with HTTP 400
`Invalid Redirect Uri: invalid uri` - the policy applies from then on.

### How to Reproduce?

```shell
# Keycloak, $T and api() as in the reproduction above
api POST "" --data '{"realm":"repro2","enabled":true}'
api PUT /repro2/client-policies/profiles --data '{"profiles":[{"name":"secure-redirects","executors":[{"executor":"secure-redirect-uris-enforcer","configuration":{}}]}]}'
api PUT /repro2/client-policies/policies --data '{"policies":[{"name":"marked-clients","enabled":true,"conditions":[{"condition":"client-attributes","configuration":{"is_negative_logic":false,"attributes":"[{\"key\":\"example.marked\",\"value\":\"true\"}]"}}],"profiles":["secure-redirects"]}]}'

api POST /repro2/clients --data '{"clientId":"marked","redirectUris":["http://app.example/*"],"attributes":{"example.marked":"true"}}'
# -> HTTP 201 (expected 400)
id=$(curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $T" "$KC/admin/realms/repro2/clients?clientId=marked" | sed -n 's/^\[{"id":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p')
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $T" "$KC/admin/realms/repro2/clients/$id" > marked.json
api PUT /repro2/clients/$id --data @marked.json
# -> HTTP 400 {"error":"invalid_request","error_description":"Invalid Redirect Uri: invalid uri"}
```

### Anything else?

We use the condition to give native apps (RFC 8252 loopback redirects) a policy of their own; until this is fixed,
new clients are checked only from their first update on.

### Describe the bug

A client policy with the condition `client-attributes` is not applied on the `REGISTER` event: a client created with
the matching attribute passes the policy's executors. The first update of the same client, even unchanged, is checked
and rejected. So a client that violates the policy can be created and then keeps working (until someone saves it).

`ClientAttributesCondition.applyPolicy` only looks at `PRE_AUTHORIZATION_REQUEST` and at a `ClientModelContext`;
when the client is created there is no populated client model yet, so the condition votes `NO` instead of evaluating
the attributes of the proposed `ClientRepresentation`. Related, same cause for workflows: #51594 (the client is not
populated yet when its creation event fires).

### Version

26.8.1 (also 26.8.0)

### Regression

- [ ] The issue is a regression

### Expected behavior

creating a client whose attributes match the condition runs the policy's executors, as the
conditions `any-client` or `client-access-type` do - here: the client with an insecure redirect URI is rejected
(HTTP 400 "Invalid Redirect Uri").

### Actual behavior

the client is created (HTTP 201). Saving it unchanged right afterwards fails with HTTP 400
`Invalid Redirect Uri: invalid uri` - the policy applies from then on.

### How to Reproduce?

```shell
# Keycloak, $T and api() as in the reproduction above
api POST "" --data '{"realm":"repro2","enabled":true}'
api PUT /repro2/client-policies/profiles --data '{"profiles":[{"name":"secure-redirects","executors":[{"executor":"secure-redirect-uris-enforcer","configuration":{}}]}]}'
api PUT /repro2/client-policies/policies --data '{"policies":[{"name":"marked-clients","enabled":true,"conditions":[{"condition":"client-attributes","configuration":{"is_negative_logic":false,"attributes":"[{\"key\":\"example.marked\",\"value\":\"true\"}]"}}],"profiles":["secure-redirects"]}]}'

api POST /repro2/clients --data '{"clientId":"marked","redirectUris":["http://app.example/*"],"attributes":{"example.marked":"true"}}'
# -> HTTP 201 (expected 400)
id=$(curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $T" "$KC/admin/realms/repro2/clients?clientId=marked" | sed -n 's/^\[{"id":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p')
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $T" "$KC/admin/realms/repro2/clients/$id" > marked.json
api PUT /repro2/clients/$id --data @marked.json
# -> HTTP 400 {"error":"invalid_request","error_description":"Invalid Redirect Uri: invalid uri"}
```

### Anything else?

We use the condition to give native apps (RFC 8252 loopback redirects) a policy of their own; until this is fixed,
new clients are checked only from their first update on.", "language": "Java", "state": "open", "assignees": [], "locked": false, "verified_at": "2026-10-22T17:42:10.762Z", "expires_at": "2026-10-23T17:42:10.762000+00:00", "timeline_complete": true, "bucket": "historical_signal_only"}

### Before reporting an issue

- [x] I have read and understood the above terms for submitting issues, and I understand that my issue may be closed without action if I do not follow them.

### Area

dist/quarkus

### Describe the bug

This is the exact same behaviour as fixed by pull request https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/51032 but applied to the management interface.

Requests to management interface health and metrics endpoint results with HTTP Status 400 when running behind a reverse proxy and having `http-management-host=127.0.0.1` (or just `http-host=127.0.0.1` which implies the same).

### Version

26.8.1

### Regression

- [x] The issue is a regression

### Expected behavior

Requests to /health or /metrics ends with HTTP Status 400

### Actual behavior

To get a valid response with HTTP Status 200

### How to Reproduce?

Enable health and / or metrics endpoint in `keycloak.conf`:
- `health-enabled=true`
- `metrics-enabled=true`

Set Keycloak to only accept request to the management interface from localhost (running behind a reverse proxy on the same host):
- `http-management-host=127.0.0.1`
-  or `http-host=127.0.0.1` which implies the same as above
- `hostname-strict=false`

### Anything else?

By setting the Quarkus property `quarkus.management.host-validation.require-localhost = false` in `quarkus.properties` the behaviour is back to the old one without having the proxy setting header `Host=localhost`. This is the exact same setting as applied in pull request https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/51032 but for the management interface.

body_text:
### Description

* Introduce a new config option `pqc-mode`.
   * Values will be `enabled`, `transitional` and `enforced`; see https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/49851#issuecomment-6163763555.
   * While `enabled` will be the default, we should log a warning if `pqc-mode=enabled` was explicitly set but no PQC crypto is available (e.g. because an older Java version is used).
* Determine, what are the default key exchange groups used by the JDK SSL engine if nothing is explicitly configured.
* Research, which PQC key exchange groups do we want to support in the beginning. This should cover both hybrid and pure PQC algorithms.
* Map `pqc-mode` values to `quarkus.tls.key-exchange-groups`.
   * `enabled`: probably no need to configure anything as PQC should be optionally supported OOTB; **this needs verification if that's true** (see the bullet point above).
   * `transitional`: change order of the default groups so that PQCs are first; optionally add missing groups based on the research (see the bullet point above); this list should contain PQC hybrid, pure as well as non-PQC algorithms.
   * `enforced`: the groups need to contain only pure PQC algorithms.
* Double check `quarkus.tls.key-exchange-groups` affects both incoming as well as outgoing (via the new Vert.x based HTTP client) connections. Add tests for it.
* Wrap it in a new experimental Feature named `pqc`.

#### Other considerations
* We will be purely relying on the JDK SSL engine, not OpenSSL. This means this will require Java 27+ until PQC is backported to OpenJDK 25.
* `pqc-mode` will be respected by other components in the future, e.g. JDBC drivers (through `jdk.tls.namedGroups` system property or similar JDK-native way).
* Reporting when non-PQC algorithms are used (as outlined in https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/49851#issuecomment-6163724090) is out of scope for this issue.
* `quarkus.tls.pqc-enforcement-policy` won't be used as that requires OpenSSL and similar effect can be achieved just via `quarkus.tls.key-exchange-groups`.
* We might consider temporarily dropping the `enforced` mode before making PQC Modes supported in case there are uncertainties around the selection of pure PQC algorithms.
* See also https://quarkus.io/guides/tls-registry-reference/#post-quantum-cryptography-pqc.

### Description

Keycloak should report when a non-PQC algorithm is used to help administrators identify areas that need adding the PQC support before starting enforcing PQC.
* Reporting will be using the logging system. When a non-PQC algorithm is detected, log a warning message.
* It will be category based so that the logging can be fine-tuned.
* Reports would be "cached" locally to avoid emitting duplicit reports. A key for the cache would basically be the "Connection ID", see the next bullet point.
   * The eviction time and cache size should be configurable. E.g. `pqc-report-interval` and `pqc-report-store-size`.
* Logging should be based on a "Connection ID".
   * E.g. emit a warning when a specific IdP used non-PQC algo in outgoing connections, i.e. the Connection ID would be a combination of IdP ID + the information it's outgoing connection for that IdP. Another Connection ID might be Client ID + a login flow type to emit warning when users are logging in via non-PQC connection. I.e. we would log a separate message for each connection type (login flow, outgoing connection etc.) and the resource that is doing it. E.g. 2 separate warnings would be emitted for a single Client where non-PQC algo would be used for its keys and TLS connection during login flow.
   * On top of Connection ID, there should also be a "Category" (e.g. `browsers`, `db`), so that the resulting category/package for the log message can be something like `org.keycloak.pqc.report.db`.
   * Realm name needs to be considered as well.
* Reporting will be enabled only with `pqc-mode=transitional` (see #54160). It can be disabled via standard log level settings.
* By default, only non-PQC algorithms will be reported. This can be made more strict by reporting also hybrid key exchange algorithms, e.g. by setting `pqc-report=strict`. This can be a follow-up.
* The reporting will be wrapped in `pqc` experimental Feature (same as #54160).
* See https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/49851#issuecomment-6163724090 for details.

#### Scope of this issue
* Implement reporting incoming and outgoing (when the new Vert.x-based client is used) HTTP connections.
   * Identify Connection IDs for each of them.
   * This can be split into multiple issues if this turns out to be too big in the end.
* Create a centralized way to conditionally emit a log message when non-PQC is used. Something like `PQC.report(algorithm, connectionId, category, realmName)`.
   * The decision whether an algorithm is PQC-safe or not (and therefore whether a log message should be emitted) should be done in `PQC.report`.
   * This could be later also used for getting the configured PQC Mode, e.g. `PQC.getMode()`. Also it could provide the list of approved algorithms/groups, e.g. `PQC.getTLSKeyExchangeGroups()`.

#### Out of scope
* Reporting on anything non-TLS related, like Realm Keys.

### Description

In the Admin Console, under a client's **Authorization** tab, the detail pages for Resources, Policies and Permissions all show a **Cancel** button next to **Save** that takes you back to the corresponding list. The detail page for an existing authorization **Scope** is the odd one out: it only offers **Revert**, which resets the form fields but does not leave the page. The only way back to the Scopes list is the browser back button or the breadcrumb.

Add a **Cancel** button to the scope edit form that navigates back to the Scopes sub-tab, matching the other three authorization detail pages. The create form already has it.

### Value Proposition

Consistent navigation across the four authorization detail pages. Users editing a scope get the same "leave without saving" affordance they already have for resources, policies and permissions.

### Goals

- Show a Cancel button on the authorization scope edit form, next to Save and Revert, that navigates to the client's Authorization → Scopes sub-tab without saving.
- Keep the existing Revert button, so the edit form offers Save, Revert and Cancel.
- Cover the behaviour with a Playwright test in the admin-ui test suite.

### Non-Goals

- Changing the behaviour of Revert.
- Changing the Resources, Policies or Permissions detail pages.
- Adding an unsaved-changes confirmation dialog.

### Discussion

_No response_

### Notes

`js/apps/admin-ui/src/clients/authorization/ScopeDetails.tsx` currently renders Cancel only while `scope` is undefined (create mode) and swaps it for Revert once the scope has loaded. The fix renders the same `Link`-based Cancel button that `ResourceDetails.tsx` uses unconditionally and keeps Revert conditional on an existing scope.
