# -> b'A\x00B\n'

backend.grep("apple", path="/tmp/p")
# GrepResult(error="Path '/tmp/p': /tmp/p/data.txt3:apple 99", matches=None)
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)

```shell
No exception is raised — that is what makes this dangerous. `grep` returns a `GrepResult` with `error` set and `matches=None`, so the tool layer surfaces `status="error"` on every successful search:


ToolMessage(name="grep", status="error",
            content="Path '/artifacts': /artifacts/data.txt3:apple 99")
```

### Description

`BaseSandbox.grep()` frames grep output with a NUL byte and parses on it:

```python
# libs/deepagents/deepagents/backends/sandbox.py
grep_opts = "-rHnFZ"                   # -Z => path\0lineno:text
file_path, rest = line.split("\0", 1)  # _parse_grep_output
```

`BaseSandbox.execute()` carries **no documented requirement that stdout preserve NUL bytes**, and `ExecuteResponse.output` is typed `str`. On any backend whose transport is text-only the NUL is dropped: every match line fails `split("\0", 1)`, `matches` stays empty, and `_parse_grep_output` returns `GrepResult(error=...)`.

The result is a **silent, total failure of grep** — a successful search is reported to the model as an error, with the matches mangled into the error string.

Not hypothetical: this is the behaviour of the in-repo Daytona backend (`libs/partners/daytona`), whose log API returns `stdout: str`.

**Both** grep paths on `main` @ `ddce7c3` emit NUL, so every grep is affected there:

1. `grep -rHnFZ ...` — the `-Z` flag (no glob / basename glob)
2. `_GREP_PATH_GLOB_TEMPLATE` — writes `chr(0)` explicitly (slash-containing glob)

### On the fix

The obvious fix is wrong: **you cannot just drop `-Z` and split on `:`.** `path:lineno:text` is ambiguous, and both regex directions fail:

| Input | non-greedy `^(.*?):(\d+):(.*)$` | greedy `^(.*):(\d+):(.*)$` |
|---|---|---|
| `/x.txt:7:key: value: 3` (colons in **text**) | ok | breaks |
| `/t:12:x.txt:9:payload` (colons in **path**) | breaks | ok |

Dropping `-Z` reintroduces #3470 in one direction or corrupts matched text in the other. The NUL delimiter was right; it just cannot survive a text transport.

A fix preserving every existing guarantee: **keep `-Z` and base64-encode the output inside the sandbox**, decoding in `_parse_grep_output`:

```
{ grep -rHnFZ ... 2>/dev/null || true; } | base64 | tr -d '\n'
```

Verified on a live Daytona sandbox with the pathological filename `/tmp/g/t:12:x.txt` — path, line number and colon-containing text all parse exactly. Transport-agnostic (fixes any text-only backend), no new dependency (`base64` is coreutils, and this file already base64-encodes params in `_GLOB_COMMAND_TEMPLATE` / `_GREP_PATH_GLOB_TEMPLATE`), and applies to both NUL paths.

Sniffing for base64 would **not** be safe — a hit whose entire output is literally `abcd` is valid base64 — so encode and decode must both be unconditional.

I have a patch ready (all `tests/unit_tests/backends/` green, `ruff` clean). Per the contribution note I have not opened a fix PR — happy to contribute a failing test, or the full fix, if a maintainer assigns this.

 #4546 

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)

```python
import asyncio
from typing import Any

from deepagents import create_deep_agent
from deepagents.backends import FilesystemBackend
from langchain_core.language_models.fake_chat_models import GenericFakeChatModel
from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage
from langchain_core.tools import tool
from langchain_quickjs import CodeInterpreterMiddleware


class ScriptedModel(GenericFakeChatModel):
    """Stands in for a model that batched two eval calls into one turn."""

    def bind_tools(self, tools: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> "ScriptedModel":
        return self

  
async def main(workspace: str) -> None:
    @tool
    async def slow_tool() -> str:
        """Take a moment, so the sibling eval starts while this one awaits."""
        await asyncio.sleep(2)
        return "done"

    middleware = CodeInterpreterMiddleware(mode="thread", ptc=["slow_tool"])
    print(middleware.tools[0].description)

    model = ScriptedModel(
        messages=iter([
            AIMessage(content="", tool_calls=[
                {"name": "eval", "args": {"code": "await tools.slowTool({})"}, "id": "a"},
                {"name": "eval", "args": {"code": "2 + 2"}, "id": "b"},
            ]),
            AIMessage(content="done"),
        ])
    )
    agent = create_deep_agent(
        model=model,
        tools=[slow_tool],
        backend=FilesystemBackend(root_dir=workspace, virtual_mode=True),
        middleware=[middleware],
    )
    result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "go"}]})
    for message in result["messages"]:
        if message.type == "tool":
            print(f"{message.tool_call_id}: {message.content}")


asyncio.run(main("/tmp/ws"))
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)

```shell
a: <result>done</result>
b: <error type="ConcurrentEval">another eval_async is already in flight on this context; use a separate context for concurrent JS workloads</error>
```

### Description

`_aeval_async` declines to queue overlapping evals on [purpose](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/blob/main/libs/partners/quickjs/langchain_quickjs/_repl.py#L780-L782):

```
Execute JavaScript in a sandboxed REPL. Persistent state is enabled: variables and
functions defined in one call are visible to subsequent calls in this conversation.
No filesystem, network, or real clock. Top-level `await` is supported; a
final-expression Promise resolves before the call returns.
```

That is a reasonable position, but the rule is nowhere the model can read it. The rendered description (above) does not mention it and `CodeInterpreterMiddleware` takes no description override. So a model that batches two eval calls learns the rule by failing and spending a turn recovering.

As a current workaround we append the description in our [uipath-langchain integration](https://uipath.github.io/uipath-python/langchain/quick_start/):
https://github.com/UiPath/uipath-langchain-python/pull/1081. 

Suggested fix: add an explanatory sentence to the rendered description.

export DEEPAGENTS_CODE_DEBUG=1

dcode \
  --model "openai:${MODEL_ID}" \
  --model-params '{"use_responses_api":false}' \
  --sandbox e2b \
  --no-mcp \

### Description

E2B is self-hosted on two local servers (control plane and sandbox server). A single non-interactive run leaves its sandbox alive: after dcode exits, the Firecracker microVM is still running on the sandbox server. It is destroyed a few minutes later, when the E2B sandbox timeout expires — not by dcode.

Expected: create_sandbox in integrations/sandbox_factory.py deletes the sandbox in its finally block when it created it (should_cleanup = sandbox_id is None), so the sandbox should go away when the run ends.

Actual: the delete is never issued. The sandbox is created in the langgraph server process (server_graph.py), which registers cleanup via atexit. The CLI stops that server with killpg(pgid, SIGTERM) (client/launch/server.py). CPython installs a handler for SIGINT but leaves SIGTERM at SIG_DFL, so the server is terminated by the kernel without running atexit, and provider.delete() never fires. Changing that signal to SIGINT in _terminate_server_process makes the sandbox disappear immediately, which confirms the path.

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)

```python
# pip install "deepagents==0.7.15" "langchain-quickjs==0.3.7"
# python main.py complete    -> exits
# python main.py interrupt   -> never exits
# python main.py error       -> never exits
# python main.py interrupt --workaround   -> exits (REPL closed from atexit)
import atexit
import sys

from deepagents import create_deep_agent
from langchain_core.language_models.fake_chat_models import GenericFakeChatModel
from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage
from langchain_core.tools import tool
from langchain_quickjs import CodeInterpreterMiddleware
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver
from langgraph.types import interrupt


class ScriptedModel(GenericFakeChatModel):
    def bind_tools(self, tools, **kwargs):
        return self


@tool
def ask_human(question: str) -> str:
    """Suspend the run until a human answers."""
    return interrupt({"question": question})


@tool
def broken_tool(x: str) -> str:
    """Always fails."""
    raise RuntimeError("boom")


scenario = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "interrupt"
second = {"complete": None, "interrupt": "ask_human", "error": "broken_tool"}[scenario]

# Turn 1 runs `eval`, which creates the REPL. Turn 2 ends the run the way the scenario says.
scripted = [
    AIMessage(content="", tool_calls=[{"id": "c1", "name": "eval", "args": {"code": "1 + 1"}}])
]
if second:
    args = {"question": "ok?"} if second == "ask_human" else {"x": "1"}
    scripted.append(AIMessage(content="", tool_calls=[{"id": "c2", "name": second, "args": args}]))
scripted.append(AIMessage(content="done"))

middleware = CodeInterpreterMiddleware(ptc=[], timeout=5.0)
if "--workaround" in sys.argv:
    # Close the REPL while its worker thread can still run. Left to __del__, the
    # close happens during interpreter finalization and blocks forever.
    atexit.register(middleware._registry.close)

agent = create_deep_agent(
    model=ScriptedModel(messages=iter(scripted)),
    tools=[ask_human, broken_tool],
    middleware=[middleware],
    checkpointer=MemorySaver(),
)

try:
    result = agent.invoke(
        {"messages": [("user", "go")]},
        config={"configurable": {"thread_id": "t1"}},
    )
    ended = "interrupted" if "__interrupt__" in result else result["messages"][-1].content
    print("run ended:", ended, flush=True)
except Exception as e:
    print("run failed:", type(e).__name__, e, flush=True)

print("exiting", flush=True)
# Without --workaround, the interrupt and error scenarios never terminate from here.
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)

```shell
N/A
```

### Description

When a run ends normally the middleware releases its QuickJS REPL, but when the graph exits through a human-in-the-loop `interrupt()` or a tool exception the REPL is kept alive. Its cleanup then only happens in `__del__` at interpreter shutdown, where it blocks on the middleware's worker thread with no timeout, and the process never terminates. The attached script shows all three endings, and --workaround shows the process exiting once the REPL is closed from an atexit hook instead.

Suggested fix: release the REPL on interrupt and exception paths as well (a finally around the turn), skip the cleanup in `__del__` when the interpreter is finalizing, bound the wait with a timeout, and expose a public `close() / aclose()` so hosts can release it deliberately.

Workaround we have to ship meanwhile: UiPath/uipath-langchain-python#1099.

The classifier-backed Auto mode approval implementation currently lives in `deepagents_code.auto_mode`. Other Deep Agents applications, including Open SWE, could use the same authorization and enforcement behavior without depending on the dcode application.

## Proposal

Extract reusable approval middleware into the Deep Agents SDK, and have dcode consume it through an application-specific adapter.

The shared implementation should own structured allow/deny decisions and validation, batch classification and deadlines, fail-closed handling, checkpoint/resume behavior, denial tool results, human-review fallback, and review lifecycle events.

Applications should supply the classifier model, trusted user authorization evidence, execution-environment context, policy and deterministic allowances, and approval-mode/UI integration. Keep dcode-specific model configuration, consent receipts, local filesystem shortcuts, scratch tools, and UI handling in dcode.

## Fleet integration requirements

- Support remote execution environments. Current deterministic checks use local `Path.resolve()` and local Git metadata; Fleet uses a sandbox-backed `CompositeBackend`. Host filesystem checks must not be used to authorize sandbox paths. Fleet could initially omit filesystem shortcuts and classify those actions.
- Accept application-validated consent separately from untrusted context. Authenticated user requests and approval answers can authorize actions; repository content, fetched Slack messages, and tool output cannot independently grant consent. Do not assume every `HumanMessage` is trusted user authorization.
- Cover subagent execution and dynamically exposed tools, not only parent-agent calls.
- Allow applications to present and resume human approval requests without depending on the dcode TUI.

## Suggested rollout

1. Extract the complete approval middleware and migrate dcode while preserving existing behavior.
2. Add Fleet integration through its existing `create_deep_agent(..., middleware=...)` construction, with Fleet-specific consent and sandbox context.

Extracting only the classifier would be smaller, but would require each consumer to reimplement enforcement, persistence, and human fallback. Sharing the complete middleware is preferred.

## Acceptance criteria

- A non-dcode Deep Agents application can install the middleware without importing `deepagents_code`.
- Existing dcode approval behavior remains covered by regression tests.
- Tests cover malformed classifier responses, timeouts, mixed allow/deny batches, checkpoint/resume, consent provenance, and subagent/dynamic-tool coverage.
- Local filesystem assumptions are isolated from remote-backend integrations.

### Submission checklist

- [x] This is a feature request for safer memory defaults and loading controls, not a usage question.
- [x] I searched existing issues; related context-budget and retrieval requests are linked below, but this request specifically addresses the eager *write guidance* plus eager *loading* together.
- [x] I checked the SDK implementation and existing configurability.
- [x] This request applies to deepagents (SDK).

### Area (Required)

- [x] deepagents (SDK)
- [ ] dcode
- [ ] talon
- [ ] acp
- [ ] evals
- [ ] daytona
- [ ] modal
- [ ] quickjs
- [ ] runloop
- [ ] vercel
- [ ] langsmith-sandbox
- [ ] Other / not sure / general

### Feature description

An agent using `MemoryMiddleware` accumulated learnings in `AGENTS.md` over a couple of weeks; the file reportedly grew to >200k tokens and was injected into the system prompt on every run. The operator moved details into skills and shortened the hot file, which should reduce context and latency. This was the **pre-MDA Content Studio** instance, not a Managed Deep Agents deployment. Reported trace (access may be limited): https://smith.langchain.com/o/ebbaf2eb-769b-4505-aca2-d11de10372a4/projects/p/9b0ca8d8-6aed-4afd-ae8d-17dec2350417?trace_id=01a0c119-56c0-7723-84c0-a90b5fb83e6d&run_id=01a0c119-56c0-7723-84c0-a90b5fb83e6d

This is consistent with the SDK's current behavior: `MEMORY_SYSTEM_PROMPT` says learning is a top priority and encourages promptly calling `edit_file` even for implicit preferences and discovered patterns. `MemoryMiddleware` loads every configured source in full, then inserts its contents into the system message for each model call, with no size or token-budget limit. Repeated small writes to always-loaded `AGENTS.md` can therefore cause escalating per-call prompt cost and latency, eventually reaching model context limits. This is a feedback loop, not just a large-file read problem.

Note: `MemoryMiddleware(system_prompt=...)` already supports a custom prompt (and `None` disables prompt injection); SDK callers can also supply middleware directly. The ask is not to add an identical parameter. Instead, make it easier to configure a *less eager memory-writing policy* in the high-level `create_deep_agent(memory=...)` path (or reconsider the default), and give applications a scalable alternative to always injecting all configured memory.

### Proposed solution (optional)

- Provide a high-level, documented opt-in choice between proactive auto-saving, saving only when explicitly asked, and loading memory without auto-save guidance. Retain backwards compatibility where needed; clearly separate a prompt-only policy from filesystem write permissions. The SDK's existing `system_prompt` override and dcode's `memory.auto_save` behavior could inform the design.
- Allow a small, bounded hot index (or no preloaded content), with details read from cold files on demand / progressively disclosed. A per-source size or token budget with an actionable error is another safety boundary. Avoid silently truncating user-authored instructions.
- Document how to pair these controls so durable learnings do not all accumulate in an always-loaded `AGENTS.md`.

Related work: #5720 covers a context-budget/liveness boundary and source ownership; #4202 proposes semantic retrieval instead of whole-file loading; #2460 discussed the over-prioritized memory prompt; merged #4700 added a prompt-level `memory.auto_save` switch in dcode. This issue focuses on the combination experienced by an SDK-backed agent, including high-level prompt-policy ergonomics and progressive loading. If maintainers prefer, it can be folded into those existing issues.

### Additional context (optional)

The shared trace link was supplied by the affected operator. Its project returned 403 through the configured LangSmith integration, so the >200k-token size, latency impact, and post-cleanup improvement are reported observations, not independently verified trace measurements here.

- [x] This is a feature request for safer memory defaults and loading controls, not a usage question.
- [x] I searched existing issues; related context-budget and retrieval requests are linked below, but this request specifically addresses the eager *write guidance* plus eager *loading* together.

- [x] This request applies to deepagents (SDK).

### Area (Required)

- [x] deepagents (SDK)
- [ ] dcode

- [ ] evals
- [ ] daytona
- [ ] modal
- [ ] quickjs
- [ ] runloop
- [ ] vercel
- [ ] langsmith-sandbox
- [ ] Other / not sure / general

### Feature description

An agent using `MemoryMiddleware` accumulated learnings in `AGENTS.md` over a couple of weeks; the file reportedly grew to >200k tokens and was injected into the system prompt on every run. The operator moved details into skills and shortened the hot file, which should reduce context and latency. This was the **pre-MDA Content Studio** instance, not a Managed Deep Agents deployment. Reported trace (access may be limited): https://smith.langchain.com/o/ebbaf2eb-769b-4505-aca2-d11de10372a4/projects/p/9b0ca8d8-6aed-4afd-ae8d-17dec2350417?trace_id=01a0c119-56c0-7723-84c0-a90b5fb83e6d&run_id=01a0c119-56c0-7723-84c0-a90b5fb83e6d

This is consistent with the SDK's current behavior: `MEMORY_SYSTEM_PROMPT` says learning is a top priority and encourages promptly calling `edit_file` even for implicit preferences and discovered patterns. `MemoryMiddleware` loads every configured source in full, then inserts its contents into the system message for each model call, with no size or token-budget limit. Repeated small writes to always-loaded `AGENTS.md` can therefore cause escalating per-call prompt cost and latency, eventually reaching model context limits. This is a feedback loop, not just a large-file read problem.

Note: `MemoryMiddleware(system_prompt=...)` already supports a custom prompt (and `None` disables prompt injection); SDK callers can also supply middleware directly. The ask is not to add an identical parameter. Instead, make it easier to configure a *less eager memory-writing policy* in the high-level `create_deep_agent(memory=...)` path (or reconsider the default), and give applications a scalable alternative to always injecting all configured memory.

### Proposed solution (optional)

- Provide a high-level, documented opt-in choice between proactive auto-saving, saving only when explicitly asked, and loading memory without auto-save guidance. Retain backwards compatibility where needed; clearly separate a prompt-only policy from filesystem write permissions. The SDK's existing `system_prompt` override and dcode's `memory.auto_save` behavior could inform the design.
- Allow a small, bounded hot index (or no preloaded content), with details read from cold files on demand / progressively disclosed. A per-source size or token budget with an actionable error is another safety boundary. Avoid silently truncating user-authored instructions.
- Document how to pair these controls so durable learnings do not all accumulate in an always-loaded `AGENTS.md`.

Related work: #5720 covers a context-budget/liveness boundary and source ownership; #4202 proposes semantic retrieval instead of whole-file loading; #2460 discussed the over-prioritized memory prompt; merged #4700 added a prompt-level `memory.auto_save` switch in dcode. This issue focuses on the combination experienced by an SDK-backed agent, including high-level prompt-policy ergonomics and progressive loading. If maintainers prefer, it can be folded into those existing issues.

### Additional context (optional)

The shared trace link was supplied by the affected operator. Its project returned 403 through the configured LangSmith integration, so the >200k-token size, latency impact, and post-cleanup improvement are reported observations, not independently verified trace measurements here.

Filed on behalf of @sydney-runkle, at her request, following a discussion with the Managed Deep Agents (MDA) team.

### Area

- [x] deepagents (SDK)

### Issue Content

Revisit the prompt-cache boundary in `MemoryMiddleware` and how it composes with provider-aware prompt caching. MDA's proposed memory middleware copies Deep Agents' Anthropic-only cache-control logic and emits ordinary text for other providers. That avoids sending Anthropic markers to unsupported providers, but does not settle caching behavior for the other models developers can select.

MDA has shared agent memory and private user memory, with per-run `allow` callbacks deciding which layers are mounted. Its proposed loader refreshes content before each model call and injects it into the request without checkpointing a `memory_contents` field. Content can therefore differ between callers/runs and after writes within a run.

### Questions / desired outcome

- Evaluate cache boundaries around stable instructions versus changing memory. Quantify cache reads/writes and cost rather than assuming caching memory is always good or always bad.
- Review middleware ordering and interaction with other cache markers, including Anthropic breakpoint limits and TTL configuration.
- Account for provider differences: Anthropic explicit markers, OpenAI automatic prefix caching, and Gemini's distinct explicit-cache lifecycle. Unsupported providers should continue to receive valid requests.
- Decide which behavior belongs in a generalized caching middleware versus memory-specific assembly; document supported providers and no-op behavior clearly.
- Test unchanged memory, edited memory, switched callers, and denied/removed layers. Cache decisions must not bypass current-run memory authorization.

### Related work

- https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/issues/3239 — **Generalize caching**. This issue is the memory-specific behavior/design follow-up, not just the rename/dispatch scaffolding described there.
- https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/issues/3639 — prior closed report about memory cache-marker placement; revisit the tradeoffs without assuming all claims in that report are established.
- https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/issues/6122 — memory refresh policy.

### Feature description

There is no eval for agents with many skills. The skill evals use one to three skills, and the Harbor `dcode` graph runs with skills turned off. But picking a skill gets hard only when there are many of them and some look alike.

On our testbed (a deepagents assistant with 236 skills), the right skill reached the model in only 55% of turns with the full list in the prompt. That is one testbed and one model, so an eval here would show whether it holds more widely.

### Proposed solution (optional)

About 50 English skills, some of them near-duplicates, and questions whose answer depends on a rule inside one skill, so code can check the answer. Record whether the right skill reached the model, whether the answer was correct, and input tokens per turn.

This gives a baseline for the default `SkillsMiddleware` and for any way of selecting skills, like pinned skills in #6338.

We can build it from our testbed. Should it be a pytest eval in `tests/evals/` or a Harbor dataset?

### Additional context (optional)

Our results: https://github.com/deyna256/langchain-skill-router#results

### Related Issues / PRs

* #5766 — notes that `dcode` already tracks `_session_cost_usd` "including nested model calls", i.e. it reconstructs this itself in `libs/code` because the SDK does not surface it.
* #6209 — a hard `--max-cost` spend cap; a cap can only be as accurate as the usage it can see, and today subagent spend is invisible to anything reading agent state.


### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)

```python
"""Minimal repro: the `task` tool discards the subagent's token usage.

Run with:  python repro_subagent_usage.py
"""

from typing import Any

from deepagents import create_deep_agent
from langchain_core.callbacks import CallbackManagerForLLMRun
from langchain_core.language_models import BaseChatModel
from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage, BaseMessage
from langchain_core.outputs import ChatGeneration, ChatResult

PARENT_TOKENS = 100
SUBAGENT_TOKENS = 5000


class ScriptedModel(BaseChatModel):
    """Replies from a script, reporting usage on every call like a real model."""

    replies: list[AIMessage]
    calls: list[int] = []

    def _generate(
        self,
        messages: list[BaseMessage],
        stop: list[str] | None = None,
        run_manager: CallbackManagerForLLMRun | None = None,
        **kwargs: Any,
    ) -> ChatResult:
        index = len(self.calls)
        self.calls.append(index)
        reply = self.replies[min(index, len(self.replies) - 1)]
        return ChatResult(generations=[ChatGeneration(message=reply)])

    def bind_tools(self, tools: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> "ScriptedModel":
        return self  # the script decides what gets called

    @property
    def _llm_type(self) -> str:
        return "scripted"


def _usage(total: int) -> dict[str, int]:
    return {"input_tokens": total, "output_tokens": 0, "total_tokens": total}


def main() -> None:
    parent = ScriptedModel(
        replies=[
            # 1. the parent delegates to the subagent…
            AIMessage(
                content="",
                tool_calls=[
                    {
                        "name": "task",
                        "args": {
                            "description": "do the work",
                            "subagent_type": "worker",
                        },
                        "id": "call-1",
                        "type": "tool_call",
                    }
                ],
                usage_metadata=_usage(PARENT_TOKENS),
            ),
            # 2. …then wraps up.
            AIMessage(content="all done", usage_metadata=_usage(PARENT_TOKENS)),
        ]
    )
    worker = ScriptedModel(
        replies=[
            AIMessage(content="worked hard", usage_metadata=_usage(SUBAGENT_TOKENS))
        ]
    )

    agent = create_deep_agent(
        model=parent,
        tools=[],
        subagents=[
            {
                "name": "worker",
                "description": "does the work",
                "prompt": "You do the work.",
                "model": worker,
            }
        ],
    )

    result = agent.invoke({"messages": [("user", "delegate this")]})

    reported = sum(
        (m.usage_metadata or {}).get("total_tokens", 0)
        for m in result["messages"]
        if isinstance(m, AIMessage)
    )
    actually_spent = PARENT_TOKENS * len(parent.calls) + SUBAGENT_TOKENS * len(
        worker.calls
    )

    tool_messages = [m for m in result["messages"] if m.type == "tool"]
    print(f"parent model calls    : {len(parent.calls)}")
    print(f"subagent model calls  : {len(worker.calls)}")
    print(f"tokens actually spent : {actually_spent}")
    print(f"tokens visible in state: {reported}")
    print(f"task ToolMessage usage : {[m.response_metadata for m in tool_messages]}")
    print()
    print(f"MISSING: {actually_spent - reported} tokens — the entire subagent spend.")

    assert worker.calls, "subagent never ran"
    assert reported < actually_spent, "usage was propagated after all"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)

```shell
No error is raised — that is the problem. Output on 0.7.19:


parent model calls    : 2
subagent model calls  : 1
tokens actually spent : 5200
tokens visible in state: 200
task ToolMessage usage : [{}]

MISSING: 5000 tokens — the entire subagent spend.


96% of the run's tokens are invisible to anything reading agent state, and the `task` `ToolMessage` carries empty `response_metadata`.
```

### Description

When the `task` tool finishes, the subagent's entire message history is reduced to a single `ToolMessage` carrying only text. Every `AIMessage.usage_metadata` produced inside the subagent is dropped at that boundary and is not recorded anywhere else.

`deepagents/middleware/subagents.py:742-755` (0.7.19):

```python
            content = ""
            for msg in reversed(result["messages"]):
                if isinstance(msg, AIMessage):
                    text = msg.text.rstrip() if msg.text else ""
                    if text:
                        content = text
                        break

        return Command(
            update={
                **state_update,
                "messages": [ToolMessage(content, tool_call_id=tool_call_id)],
            }
        )
```

`result["messages"]` holds the full subagent history, including its token counts. It is walked purely to scrape the last non-empty text, and the returned `ToolMessage` gets no `response_metadata`.

The consequence is that **any usage accounting done by summing `usage_metadata` over agent state is structurally incapable of seeing subagent spend** — and for delegation-heavy agents the subagent is where most of the tokens go, so the number isn't slightly low, it's mostly wrong. There's no error and no warning; the total just looks plausible.

To be clear about what I am *not* asking for: collapsing the subagent transcript is the entire point of the `task` tool, and forwarding those messages would defeat context isolation. Usage metadata is orthogonal to that — it's a small fixed-size dict, not context.

**Expected:** the aggregated subagent usage survives the boundary, e.g. attached to the returned `ToolMessage`'s `response_metadata`, so downstream consumers can account for it without each reinventing out-of-band tracking (as #5766 shows `dcode` having to do).

**Observed in production:** we run a delegation-heavy agent on deepagents and our per-run token reporting was understating spend by roughly half (~$3 reported against ~$6 actual on one run of 152 requests) until we worked around it with a run-scoped `BaseCallbackHandler` that catches `on_llm_end` across the whole callback tree. That workaround only works because it bypasses agent state entirely — it shouldn't be necessary.

    return {"input_tokens": total, "output_tokens": 0, "total_tokens": total}


def main() -> None:
    parent = ScriptedModel(
        replies=[
            # 1. the parent delegates to the subagent…
            AIMessage(
                content="",
                tool_calls=[
                    {
                        "name": "task",
                        "args": {
                            "description": "do the work",
                            "subagent_type": "worker",
                        },
                        "id": "call-1",
                        "type": "tool_call",
                    }
                ],
                usage_metadata=_usage(PARENT_TOKENS),
            ),
            # 2. …then wraps up.
            AIMessage(content="all done", usage_metadata=_usage(PARENT_TOKENS)),
        ]
    )
    worker = ScriptedModel(
        replies=[
            AIMessage(content="worked hard", usage_metadata=_usage(SUBAGENT_TOKENS))
        ]
    )

    agent = create_deep_agent(
        model=parent,
        tools=[],
        subagents=[
            {
                "name": "worker",
                "description": "does the work",
                "prompt": "You do the work.",
                "model": worker,
            }
        ],
    )

    result = agent.invoke({"messages": [("user", "delegate this")]})

    reported = sum(
        (m.usage_metadata or {}).get("total_tokens", 0)
        for m in result["messages"]
        if isinstance(m, AIMessage)
    )
    actually_spent = PARENT_TOKENS * len(parent.calls) + SUBAGENT_TOKENS * len(
        worker.calls
    )

    tool_messages = [m for m in result["messages"] if m.type == "tool"]
    print(f"parent model calls    : {len(parent.calls)}")
    print(f"subagent model calls  : {len(worker.calls)}")
    print(f"tokens actually spent : {actually_spent}")
    print(f"tokens visible in state: {reported}")
    print(f"task ToolMessage usage : {[m.response_metadata for m in tool_messages]}")
    print()
    print(f"MISSING: {actually_spent - reported} tokens — the entire subagent spend.")

    assert worker.calls, "subagent never ran"
    assert reported < actually_spent, "usage was propagated after all"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)

```shell
No error is raised — that is the problem. Output on 0.7.19:


parent model calls    : 2
subagent model calls  : 1
tokens actually spent : 5200
tokens visible in state: 200
task ToolMessage usage : [{}]

MISSING: 5000 tokens — the entire subagent spend.


96% of the run's tokens are invisible to anything reading agent state, and the `task` `ToolMessage` carries empty `response_metadata`.
```

### Description

When the `task` tool finishes, the subagent's entire message history is reduced to a single `ToolMessage` carrying only text. Every `AIMessage.usage_metadata` produced inside the subagent is dropped at that boundary and is not recorded anywhere else.

`deepagents/middleware/subagents.py:742-755` (0.7.19):

```python
            content = ""
            for msg in reversed(result["messages"]):
                if isinstance(msg, AIMessage):
                    text = msg.text.rstrip() if msg.text else ""
                    if text:
                        content = text
                        break

        return Command(
            update={
                **state_update,
                "messages": [ToolMessage(content, tool_call_id=tool_call_id)],
            }
        )
```

`result["messages"]` holds the full subagent history, including its token counts. It is walked purely to scrape the last non-empty text, and the returned `ToolMessage` gets no `response_metadata`.

The consequence is that **any usage accounting done by summing `usage_metadata` over agent state is structurally incapable of seeing subagent spend** — and for delegation-heavy agents the subagent is where most of the tokens go, so the number isn't slightly low, it's mostly wrong. There's no error and no warning; the total just looks plausible.

To be clear about what I am *not* asking for: collapsing the subagent transcript is the entire point of the `task` tool, and forwarding those messages would defeat context isolation. Usage metadata is orthogonal to that — it's a small fixed-size dict, not context.

**Expected:** the aggregated subagent usage survives the boundary, e.g. attached to the returned `ToolMessage`'s `response_metadata`, so downstream consumers can account for it without each reinventing out-of-band tracking (as #5766 shows `dcode` having to do).

**Observed in production:** we run a delegation-heavy agent on deepagents and our per-run token reporting was understating spend by roughly half (~$3 reported against ~$6 actual on one run of 152 requests) until we worked around it with a run-scoped `BaseCallbackHandler` that catches `on_llm_end` across the whole callback tree. That workaround only works because it bypasses agent state entirely — it shouldn't be necessary.

### Submission checklist

- [x] This is a bug, not a usage question.
- [x] I added a clear and descriptive title.
- [x] I searched existing issues and didn't find this.
- [x] I can reproduce this with the latest released version.
- [x] I included a minimal reproducible example and steps to reproduce.

### Area (Required)

- [x] deepagents (SDK)
- [x] dcode
- [ ] talon
- [ ] acp
- [ ] evals
- [ ] daytona
- [ ] modal
- [ ] quickjs
- [ ] runloop
- [ ] vercel
- [ ] langsmith-sandbox
- [ ] Other / not sure / general

### Related Issues / PRs

Related: #5720, PR #5717, #6502.

This issue is related to, but narrower than, the broader ownership problem discussed in #5720 and PR #5717:

- #5720 discusses ownership and context-budget boundaries for persistent memory.
- PR #5717 explores read-only vs writable semantics at the **source/file level**.
- This issue focuses specifically on **how project-authored instructions and learned memory are represented when they coexist inside the same `AGENTS.md` file**.
- #6502 discusses eager memory writing and bounded/progressive loading. That is a related loading-policy problem, but not the change proposed here.

### Description

`MemoryMiddleware` currently loads the full contents of an `AGENTS.md` source into `<agent_memory>`.

That is compatible with using `AGENTS.md` as persistent project context, but it creates a representation ambiguity when the same file contains both:

1. **Project/user-authored instructions**
   - repository conventions
   - build/test requirements
   - stable constraints
   - other explicitly authored project guidance

2. **Agent-learned memory**
   - preferences learned during use
   - corrections
   - reusable observations
   - other knowledge written back by the agent

These two categories have different semantics and lifecycle expectations, but today they share the same representation inside `MemoryMiddleware`.

The problem is **not** that project-authored instructions should disappear from the model context. They can be valid and useful agent-facing system context.

The problem is that there is currently no explicit representation boundary between authored instructions and agent-learned memory when both occupy the same file.

### Released behavior reproduction

I reproduced this through the real `create_cli_agent()` wiring rather than manually constructing a `MemoryMiddleware` prompt.

The released baseline uses:

```text
deepagents-code==0.1.77
source commit: dcf4febea597a876043f0aea6ecae40c321ea541
Python: 3.12.14
```

The harness uses a fake model, so no provider API key or external model is required.

It builds the real CLI agent, invokes it, and records the actual model-visible system content blocks.

#### Default memory-enabled case

`create_cli_agent()` has `enable_memory=True` by default.

The release trace uses the actual repository as the project root, so the repository `AGENTS.md` is automatically discovered:

```text
/reproduction-workspace/deepagents-release/AGENTS.md
```

The captured model-visible prompt contains repository-authored content such as:

```text
# Global development guidelines for the Deep Agents monorepo

## PR conventions

#### Warnings are errors
```

inside `<agent_memory>`.

Conceptually:

```text
<agent_memory>

/reproduction-workspace/deepagents-release/AGENTS.md

# Global development guidelines for the Deep Agents monorepo

...

## PR conventions

...

#### Warnings are errors

...

</agent_memory>
```

#### Memory-disabled control

Running the same released CLI wiring with:

```python
enable_memory=False
```

removes that memory path.

The paired trace contains no `<agent_memory>` block, and none of the three repository probes above are present.

The release pair therefore demonstrates:

```text
default CLI memory path
    → discovers project AGENTS.md
    → loads the whole file through MemoryMiddleware
    → repository-authored instructions appear inside <agent_memory>

same wiring with memory disabled
    → those contents do not enter through the memory path
```

The automatic discovery in this reproduction belongs to the CLI wiring.

The whole-file representation once a source is loaded belongs to SDK `MemoryMiddleware`.

### Why this distinction matters

Authored instructions and learned memory have different semantics.

Conceptually:

```text
project-authored instructions
    authored by: user / repository
    purpose: stable agent-facing requirements and constraints
    lifecycle: explicitly maintained

agent-learned memory
    produced by: agent during use
    purpose: reusable learned information
    lifecycle: may evolve as the agent learns
```

When both are represented as one undifferentiated memory payload, later memory lifecycle work has no explicit representation-level boundary to operate on.

For example, future work on:

- compaction;
- consolidation;
- progressive loading;
- hot/cold memory separation;
- pruning;
- migration;

would benefit from being able to identify learned memory independently from authored instructions.

This issue does **not** claim that the prototype below provides filesystem-level ownership or write protection.

It establishes a **representation / prompt boundary** only.

The broader permission and ownership problem remains covered by #5720 and PR #5717.

### Candidate representation

One compatibility-preserving option is to allow an `AGENTS.md` file to opt into an explicit learned-memory region.

For example:

```markdown
# Project instructions

Use Conventional Commits.

<!-- deepagents:memory:start -->
## Durable memory

MEMORY_SENTINEL: Prefer concise answers.
<!-- deepagents:memory:end -->

#### Warnings are errors

Run the unit tests with warnings treated as errors.
```

The intended representation is:

```text
outside the markers
    → authored system context

inside the markers
    → learned memory inside <agent_memory>
```

I implemented this candidate locally and captured it through the same real `create_cli_agent()` wiring.

The candidate traces use:

```text
combined candidate commit:
a1e276d04792b1b7fb006ddc505df6a369450d36

based on upstream:
0bacb9fb1814ec2168e35efd7f4ebba7d330d741

Python:
3.12.14
```

The proposed changes are split into PRs #6561 and #6562.

### Candidate trace: structured `AGENTS.md`

The structured fixture contains:

```markdown
# Global development guidelines for the Deep Agents monorepo

## PR conventions

Use Conventional Commits.

<!-- deepagents:memory:start -->
## Durable memory

MEMORY_SENTINEL: Prefer concise answers.
<!-- deepagents:memory:end -->

#### Warnings are errors

Run the unit tests with warnings treated as errors.
```

The captured prompt shows that:

- `Global development guidelines` remains model-visible;
- `PR conventions` remains model-visible;
- `Warnings are errors` remains model-visible;
- only the marked durable-memory content appears inside `<agent_memory>`;
- the boundary markers themselves are not exposed in the memory block.

The learned-memory block is:

```text
<agent_memory>

/reproduction-workspace/evidence-v5/fixtures/structured/AGENTS.md

## Durable memory

MEMORY_SENTINEL: Prefer concise answers.

</agent_memory>
```

The authored instructions remain present in separate system content outside that block.

This is the main behavior the candidate is intended to establish.

### Candidate trace: legacy compatibility

The legacy fixture has no markers:

```markdown
# Global development guidelines for the Deep Agents monorepo

## PR conventions

Use Conventional Commits.

## Durable memory

MEMORY_SENTINEL: Prefer concise answers.

#### Warnings are errors

Run the unit tests with warnings treated as errors.
```

Under the candidate implementation, the full file still appears inside `<agent_memory>`.

So existing unstructured files preserve the current whole-file memory-loading/classification behavior:

```text
no markers
    → whole-file memory semantics
```

The candidate therefore does not automatically reinterpret existing unmarked `AGENTS.md` files.

### Candidate trace: empty learned-memory section

The empty fixture contains:

```markdown
# Global development guidelines for the Deep Agents monorepo

## PR conventions

Use Conventional Commits.

<!-- deepagents:memory:start -->
<!-- deepagents:memory:end -->

#### Warnings are errors

Run the unit tests with warnings treated as errors.
```

The captured prompt shows that the authored instructions remain model-visible outside `<agent_memory>`.

The memory block becomes:

```text
<agent_memory>

(No memory loaded)

</agent_memory>
```

The normal memory capability guidance remains present.

This intentionally means:

```text
memory enabled + empty learned-memory section
```

is **not** identical to:

```text
memory disabled
```

An enabled memory capability can reasonably add memory-specific guidance even when there is no learned memory yet.

The issue here is the representation of authored content, not whether memory capability instructions exist.

### Summary of captured evidence

| Trace | Input and result |
| --- | --- |
| `release-default.json` | Released `deepagents-code==0.1.77`; default memory enabled; repository `AGENTS.md` automatically discovered; project development guidelines appear inside `<agent_memory>` |
| `release-disabled.json` | Same release and repository; `enable_memory=False`; those guidelines do not enter through memory |
| `patched-structured.json` | Candidate + structured fixture; authored instructions remain system-visible outside `<agent_memory>`; only `MEMORY_SENTINEL` enters the memory block |
| `patched-legacy.json` | Candidate + unmarked legacy fixture; full file retains legacy memory-loading behavior |
| `patched-empty.json` | Candidate + empty memory section; authored instructions remain visible; memory shows `(No memory loaded)` and retains memory guidance |

The first two traces form the paired released-version reproduction.

The other three test distinct candidate inputs and are not intended as byte-for-byte comparisons with the released prompt.

### Reproduction harness

The attached `capture_cli_trace.py`:

- imports the real `create_cli_agent()`;
- creates a real `ProjectContext`;
- uses `project_agent_md_paths()` for project discovery;
- constructs the actual CLI agent;
- invokes it using a `GenericFakeChatModel`;
- captures the system messages the model receives;
- records the individual model-visible content blocks;
- records discovered project paths, source commit, Python version, requested memory mode, and probe matches.

Example candidate reproduction:

```bash
python capture_cli_trace.py \
  --source-root /path/to/deepagents-at-candidate-commit \
  --project-root /path/to/fixtures/structured \
  --scratch /tmp/deepagents-memory-repro \
  --output /tmp/structured.json \
  --memory default
```

`--memory default` intentionally omits the `enable_memory` argument so the CLI default is exercised.

`--memory disabled` explicitly passes:

```python
enable_memory=False
```

For the released baseline, the release checkout is used as both `--source-root` and `--project-root`, so its real repository `AGENTS.md` is automatically discovered.

### Possible approaches

#### Option A: structured `AGENTS.md`

Keep authored instructions and learned memory in the same file, but make the learned region explicit:

```markdown
# Authored project instructions

...

<!-- deepagents:memory:start -->

learned memory

<!-- deepagents:memory:end -->

...
```

Advantages:

- minimal API change;
- existing unmarked files retain their current whole-file memory-loading/classification behavior;
- users can opt in gradually;
- authored and learned content can remain colocated.

The current candidate implements this approach.

Its writing discipline is currently prompt-based: the agent is instructed to read the file and keep learned-memory writes inside the marked section while preserving the surrounding content.

The markers do **not** enforce filesystem write permissions.

This representation also changes the prompt trust semantics of marker-external content: once it is moved outside `<agent_memory>`, it is no longer covered by the memory-specific trust and verification guidance. If authored project instructions should retain a different trust level, that may need an explicit representation of its own.

#### Option B: separate authored instructions and learned memory physically

Another approach is to use distinct storage surfaces:

```text
AGENTS.md / instruction source
    → project-authored instructions

separate memory file or tree
    → learned writable memory
```

This creates a stronger physical distinction.

It may also be a better foundation for later memory organization such as bounded hot memory plus larger on-demand memory files.

The tradeoff is a broader compatibility/API change.

I do not think the marker-based candidate must necessarily be the final design.

It is primarily a concrete implementation demonstrating that the representations can be separated while preserving legacy whole-file loading for unmarked files.

### Relationship to #5720

#5720 discusses the broader ownership and context-budget problem.

Its ownership side asks how user/application-authored instructions can be distinguished and protected from agent-owned writable memory.

PR #5717 explores that at the **source level**, including read-only vs writable source semantics.

This issue is narrower:

> If authored instructions and learned memory coexist within one `AGENTS.md`, how should they be represented separately to the model?

The candidate addresses that intra-file representation question.

It does not replace #5720's permission or context-budget work.

### Relationship to PR #5717

PR #5717 explores:

```text
read-only source
vs
writable source
```

That answers:

> Which source may the agent modify?

This issue asks:

> Within one source, which content is authored project context and which content is learned memory?

These are complementary boundaries.

The structured candidate remains prompt-enforced and does not make marker-external content technically immutable.

### Relationship to #6502

#6502 discusses:

- eager memory-writing guidance;
- memory growth;
- bounded/progressive loading.

That is a separate lifecycle/loading problem.

However, progressive loading or future hot/cold organization benefits from first identifying which content is actually learned memory.

Otherwise project-authored instructions stored in the same file may be swept into learned-memory lifecycle policies.

This issue therefore provides a representation boundary that could support later loading work without proposing that work here.

### Scope

This issue does **not** propose:

- hot/cold memory implementation;
- semantic retrieval;
- vector search;
- automatic compaction;
- token-budget handling;
- memory consolidation;
- filesystem permission enforcement;
- changing the whole-file loading/classification behavior of existing unmarked `AGENTS.md` files.

The requested design question is narrower:

> Establish an explicit representation boundary between project-authored instructions and agent-learned memory when both coexist in the same `AGENTS.md`.

### Candidate implementation

A concrete implementation is available in:

- #6561 — SDK structured-memory parsing, prompt integration, and regression tests
- #6562 — dcode prompt guidance for keeping writes inside marked memory sections

Both PRs were automatically closed by the repository contribution-policy bot because this issue had not yet been approved and assigned.

They were not closed following maintainer code review.

If maintainers prefer the structured representation, I can update/reopen the implementation after assignment.

If a physically separate instruction/memory surface is preferred, I am also happy to adapt the implementation in that direction.

The goal is not to mandate the marker syntax.

The goal is to make these two concepts distinguishable:

```text
project-authored instructions
```

and:

```text
agent-learned memory
```

within the current `AGENTS.md` workflow.

### Evidence

Attached:

`deepagents-agents-memory-evidence-clean.zip`

The archive contains:

- `README.md`
- `capture_cli_trace.py`
- `fixtures/legacy/AGENTS.md`
- `fixtures/structured/AGENTS.md`
- `fixtures/empty-section/AGENTS.md`
- `traces/release-default.json`
- `traces/release-disabled.json`
- `traces/patched-structured.json`
- `traces/patched-legacy.json`
- `traces/patched-empty.json`

The ZIP contains evidence only; it does not contain the implementation patch.

Published trace paths are normalized to:

```text
/reproduction-workspace
```

while preserving the prompt content and content-block boundaries.

### Related Issues / PRs

Related: #5720, PR #5717, #6502.

This issue is related to, but narrower than, the broader ownership problem discussed in #5720 and PR #5717:

- #5720 discusses ownership and context-budget boundaries for persistent memory.

### Description

`MemoryMiddleware` currently loads the full contents of an `AGENTS.md` source into `<agent_memory>`.

That is compatible with using `AGENTS.md` as persistent project context, but it creates a representation ambiguity when the same file contains both:

1. **Project/user-authored instructions**
   - repository conventions
   - build/test requirements
   - stable constraints
   - other explicitly authored project guidance

2. **Agent-learned memory**
   - preferences learned during use
   - corrections
   - reusable observations
   - other knowledge written back by the agent

These two categories have different semantics and lifecycle expectations, but today they share the same representation inside `MemoryMiddleware`.

The problem is **not** that project-authored instructions should disappear from the model context. They can be valid and useful agent-facing system context.

The problem is that there is currently no explicit representation boundary between authored instructions and agent-learned memory when both occupy the same file.

It builds the real CLI agent, invokes it, and records the actual model-visible system content blocks.

```text
# Global development guidelines for the Deep Agents monorepo

## PR conventions

#### Warnings are errors
```

inside `<agent_memory>`.

/reproduction-workspace/deepagents-release/AGENTS.md

# Global development guidelines for the Deep Agents monorepo

...

## PR conventions

...

#### Warnings are errors

...

</agent_memory>
```

Running the same released CLI wiring with:

```

removes that memory path.

The paired trace contains no `<agent_memory>` block, and none of the three repository probes above are present.

The release pair therefore demonstrates:

```text

    → discovers project AGENTS.md

    → repository-authored instructions appear inside <agent_memory>

same wiring with memory disabled
    → those contents do not enter through the memory path
```

The automatic discovery in this reproduction belongs to the CLI wiring.

The whole-file representation once a source is loaded belongs to SDK `MemoryMiddleware`.

### Why this distinction matters

Authored instructions and learned memory have different semantics.

Conceptually:

```text
project-authored instructions
    authored by: user / repository
    purpose: stable agent-facing requirements and constraints
    lifecycle: explicitly maintained

agent-learned memory
    produced by: agent during use
    purpose: reusable learned information
    lifecycle: may evolve as the agent learns
```

When both are represented as one undifferentiated memory payload, later memory lifecycle work has no explicit representation-level boundary to operate on.

For example, future work on:

- compaction;
- consolidation;
- progressive loading;
- hot/cold memory separation;
- pruning;
- migration;

would benefit from being able to identify learned memory independently from authored instructions.

This issue does **not** claim that the prototype below provides filesystem-level ownership or write protection.

It establishes a **representation / prompt boundary** only.

The broader permission and ownership problem remains covered by #5720 and PR #5717.

### Candidate representation

One compatibility-preserving option is to allow an `AGENTS.md` file to opt into an explicit learned-memory region.

For example:

```markdown
# Project instructions

Use Conventional Commits.

<!-- deepagents:memory:start -->
## Durable memory

MEMORY_SENTINEL: Prefer concise answers.
<!-- deepagents:memory:end -->

#### Warnings are errors

Run the unit tests with warnings treated as errors.
```

The intended representation is:

```text
outside the markers
    → authored system context

inside the markers
    → learned memory inside <agent_memory>
```

I implemented this candidate locally and captured it through the same real `create_cli_agent()` wiring.

The candidate traces use:

```text
combined candidate commit:
a1e276d04792b1b7fb006ddc505df6a369450d36

based on upstream:
0bacb9fb1814ec2168e35efd7f4ebba7d330d741

Python:
3.12.14
```

The proposed changes are split into PRs #6561 and #6562.

### Candidate trace: structured `AGENTS.md`

The structured fixture contains:

```markdown
# Global development guidelines for the Deep Agents monorepo

## PR conventions

Use Conventional Commits.

<!-- deepagents:memory:start -->
## Durable memory

MEMORY_SENTINEL: Prefer concise answers.
<!-- deepagents:memory:end -->

#### Warnings are errors

Run the unit tests with warnings treated as errors.
```

The captured prompt shows that:

- `Global development guidelines` remains model-visible;
- `PR conventions` remains model-visible;
- `Warnings are errors` remains model-visible;
- only the marked durable-memory content appears inside `<agent_memory>`;
- the boundary markers themselves are not exposed in the memory block.

The learned-memory block is:

```text
<agent_memory>

/reproduction-workspace/evidence-v5/fixtures/structured/AGENTS.md

## Durable memory

MEMORY_SENTINEL: Prefer concise answers.

</agent_memory>
```

The authored instructions remain present in separate system content outside that block.

This is the main behavior the candidate is intended to establish.

### Candidate trace: legacy compatibility

The legacy fixture has no markers:

Use Conventional Commits.

MEMORY_SENTINEL: Prefer concise answers.

#### Warnings are errors

Run the unit tests with warnings treated as errors.
```

Under the candidate implementation, the full file still appears inside `<agent_memory>`.

So existing unstructured files preserve the current whole-file memory-loading/classification behavior:

```text
no markers

```

The candidate therefore does not automatically reinterpret existing unmarked `AGENTS.md` files.

This intentionally means:

The issue here is the representation of authored content, not whether memory capability instructions exist.

### Possible approaches

#### Option A: structured `AGENTS.md`

Keep authored instructions and learned memory in the same file, but make the learned region explicit:

```markdown
# Authored project instructions

...

<!-- deepagents:memory:start -->

learned memory

<!-- deepagents:memory:end -->

...
```

Advantages:

- minimal API change;
- existing unmarked files retain their current whole-file memory-loading/classification behavior;
- users can opt in gradually;
- authored and learned content can remain colocated.

The current candidate implements this approach.

Its writing discipline is currently prompt-based: the agent is instructed to read the file and keep learned-memory writes inside the marked section while preserving the surrounding content.

The markers do **not** enforce filesystem write permissions.

This representation also changes the prompt trust semantics of marker-external content: once it is moved outside `<agent_memory>`, it is no longer covered by the memory-specific trust and verification guidance. If authored project instructions should retain a different trust level, that may need an explicit representation of its own.

#### Option B: separate authored instructions and learned memory physically

Another approach is to use distinct storage surfaces:

```text
AGENTS.md / instruction source
    → project-authored instructions

separate memory file or tree
    → learned writable memory
```

This creates a stronger physical distinction.

It may also be a better foundation for later memory organization such as bounded hot memory plus larger on-demand memory files.

The tradeoff is a broader compatibility/API change.

I do not think the marker-based candidate must necessarily be the final design.

It is primarily a concrete implementation demonstrating that the representations can be separated while preserving legacy whole-file loading for unmarked files.

### Relationship to #5720

#5720 discusses the broader ownership and context-budget problem.

Its ownership side asks how user/application-authored instructions can be distinguished and protected from agent-owned writable memory.

PR #5717 explores that at the **source level**, including read-only vs writable source semantics.

This issue is narrower:

> If authored instructions and learned memory coexist within one `AGENTS.md`, how should they be represented separately to the model?

The candidate addresses that intra-file representation question.

It does not replace #5720's permission or context-budget work.

### Relationship to PR #5717

PR #5717 explores:

```text
read-only source
vs
writable source
```

That answers:

> Which source may the agent modify?

This issue asks:

> Within one source, which content is authored project context and which content is learned memory?

These are complementary boundaries.

The structured candidate remains prompt-enforced and does not make marker-external content technically immutable.

### Relationship to #6502

#6502 discusses:

- eager memory-writing guidance;
- memory growth;
- bounded/progressive loading.

That is a separate lifecycle/loading problem.

However, progressive loading or future hot/cold organization benefits from first identifying which content is actually learned memory.

Otherwise project-authored instructions stored in the same file may be swept into learned-memory lifecycle policies.

This issue therefore provides a representation boundary that could support later loading work without proposing that work here.

### Scope

This issue does **not** propose:

- hot/cold memory implementation;
- semantic retrieval;
- vector search;
- automatic compaction;
- token-budget handling;
- memory consolidation;
- filesystem permission enforcement;
- changing the whole-file loading/classification behavior of existing unmarked `AGENTS.md` files.

The requested design question is narrower:

> Establish an explicit representation boundary between project-authored instructions and agent-learned memory when both coexist in the same `AGENTS.md`.

### Candidate implementation

A concrete implementation is available in:

- #6561 — SDK structured-memory parsing, prompt integration, and regression tests
- #6562 — dcode prompt guidance for keeping writes inside marked memory sections

Both PRs were automatically closed by the repository contribution-policy bot because this issue had not yet been approved and assigned.

They were not closed following maintainer code review.

If maintainers prefer the structured representation, I can update/reopen the implementation after assignment.

If a physically separate instruction/memory surface is preferred, I am also happy to adapt the implementation in that direction.

The goal is not to mandate the marker syntax.

The goal is to make these two concepts distinguishable:

```text
project-authored instructions
```

and:

```text
agent-learned memory
```

within the current `AGENTS.md` workflow.

### Submission checklist

- [x] This is a feature request, not a bug report.
- [x] I searched existing issues and didn't find this feature.
- [x] I checked the docs and README for existing functionality.
- [x] This request applies to this repo (deepagents) and not an external package.

### Area (Required)

- [x] deepagents (SDK)
- [ ] dcode
- [ ] talon
- [ ] acp
- [ ] evals
- [ ] daytona
- [ ] modal
- [ ] quickjs
- [ ] runloop
- [ ] vercel
- [ ] langsmith-sandbox
- [ ] Other / not sure / general

## Background

I would like to propose an opt-in contract for persistent learned memory access among subagents under the same parent.

**This is not a report that subagents cannot share memory.** Existing backend routing and per-subagent filesystem permissions can already implement several sharing arrangements.

I reviewed the Python SDK at [7bc94742bb503772e207a46d29bbd7cea13e7129](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/commit/7bc94742bb503772e207a46d29bbd7cea13e7129) on October 2, 2026. The relevant implementation is unchanged from release 0.7.21.

In the current implementation:

- Declarative subagents generally receive the same backend used by the parent’s built-in filesystem middleware ([create_deep_agent](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/blob/7bc94742bb503772e207a46d29bbd7cea13e7129/libs/deepagents/deepagents/graph.py)).
- `memory=` selects files to preload; it does not define ownership or a sharing policy ([create_deep_agent](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/blob/7bc94742bb503772e207a46d29bbd7cea13e7129/libs/deepagents/deepagents/graph.py), [MemoryMiddleware](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/blob/7bc94742bb503772e207a46d29bbd7cea13e7129/libs/deepagents/deepagents/middleware/memory.py)).
- Ordinary isolated declarative subagents do not automatically inherit the parent’s `MemoryMiddleware`; forked subagents mirror it ([agent assembly](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/blob/7bc94742bb503772e207a46d29bbd7cea13e7129/libs/deepagents/deepagents/graph.py), [SubAgent](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/blob/7bc94742bb503772e207a46d29bbd7cea13e7129/libs/deepagents/deepagents/middleware/subagents.py)).
- `StoreBackend` uses the same resolved namespace for reads and mutations, rather than separate namespace policies for readable and writable memory ([StoreBackend](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/blob/7bc94742bb503772e207a46d29bbd7cea13e7129/libs/deepagents/deepagents/backends/store.py)).
- Subagents can define their own filesystem permissions ([FilesystemMiddleware](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/blob/7bc94742bb503772e207a46d29bbd7cea13e7129/libs/deepagents/deepagents/middleware/filesystem.py), [Permissions documentation](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/permissions)).
- `MemoryMiddleware` preloads sources directly through the backend, independently of filesystem-tool permission checks ([MemoryMiddleware](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/blob/7bc94742bb503772e207a46d29bbd7cea13e7129/libs/deepagents/deepagents/middleware/memory.py)).

The existing memory model and permission primitives are described in the official [Memory documentation](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/memory) and [Permissions documentation](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/permissions).

**The missing abstraction is not sharing capability, but a single contract that keeps ownership, visibility, preload behavior, and mutation authority consistent.**

## Use case

A parent coordinates a researcher and an evaluator:

- The researcher maintains durable research learnings.
- The evaluator maintains evaluation learnings.
- Each may read the other’s explicitly shared learnings.

body_text:
## Problem

Deep Agents needs a first-class backend on its execution runtime and a supported way for deployment platforms to extend that runtime with typed capabilities, without taking over application-defined context.

`Runtime`, Agent Server's factory-facing `ServerRuntime`, and tool-facing `ToolRuntime` are distinct surfaces; this request is for a coherent contract across the relevant surfaces, not an assertion that Deep Agents owns all three implementations.

### Backend as a first-class capability

Deep Agents accepts a backend in `create_deep_agent`, but authored tools and middleware need a supported, typed way to access the backend selected for their execution, rather than independently reconstructing it or relying on platform wrappers. Backend lifecycle and propagation to subagents should be specified, including when no backend is available.

### Typed runtime extensibility

Managed Deep Agents (MDA) needs `runtime.channel` as a proper typed capability, alongside backend and server identity. Today it implements custom runtime augmentation:

- [Python managed runtime type and proxy](https://github.com/langchain-ai/managed-deepagents-sdk/blob/5c5f9124c9e2fe36cf2286d5d8f37c05f309af2e/packages/pypi/src/managed_deepagents/_managed_tools.py): `ManagedDeepAgentRuntime` declares managed fields; `_ManagedRuntime` delegates to the native runtime; `with_managed_runtime` wraps tool callables and replaces the injected runtime. It also depends on LangChain's private injected-argument marker.
- [TypeScript runtime augmentation](https://github.com/langchain-ai/managed-deepagents-sdk/blob/5c5f9124c9e2fe36cf2286d5d8f37c05f309af2e/packages/npm/src/runtime/managed-tools.ts): `ManagedDeepAgentRuntime` extends `ToolRuntime`; callable wrapping and a proxy propagate the additional fields.
- [Channel binding](https://github.com/langchain-ai/managed-deepagents-sdk/blob/5c5f9124c9e2fe36cf2286d5d8f37c05f309af2e/packages/pypi/src/managed_deepagents/_channels/binding.py) resolves delivery context into the channel capability.
- [Run context types](https://github.com/langchain-ai/managed-deepagents-sdk/blob/5c5f9124c9e2fe36cf2286d5d8f37c05f309af2e/packages/pypi/src/managed_deepagents/run_context.py) currently distinguish application context from managed channel context.

These MDA source links require access to its private repository. The problem is understandable without that access: platforms must reproduce injection/proxy behavior just to add a typed runtime property.

## Desired contract

- Preserve `Runtime[MyContext]` / `runtime.context` for application-defined typed dependencies.
- Expose the selected Deep Agents backend through a first-class typed capability on the appropriate execution runtime.
- Provide supported typed runtime extension/composition and injection hooks, so a platform can add `channel` without patching individual tool callables or relying on private framework markers.
- Keep platform delivery/source metadata separate from application dependencies. Specify how metadata and capabilities reach factories, tools, middleware, and subagents, including resume behavior and absent channel data.
- Preserve the trust boundary: inbound event data is not authenticated identity; reply routing and privileged capabilities must come from verified ingress.

An explicit capabilities/extension container could be an alternative to arbitrary top-level runtime fields; the key requirement is a supported, type-preserving mechanism, not a mandated API spelling.

## Precedent / design questions

[Eve dynamic capabilities](https://eve.dev/docs/guides/dynamic-capabilities) distinguishes channel information (`ctx.channel.kind`) from authenticated session information (`ctx.session.auth.current`) in connection resolvers. [Pydantic AI](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/core-concepts/dependencies/) separates user-defined typed dependencies (`RunContext[MyDeps].deps`) from other runtime facilities. Neither establishes the exact API Deep Agents should adopt, but both support keeping user dependency types independent of platform-owned runtime capabilities.

Which parts belong in Deep Agents versus LangGraph / LangChain / Agent Server? Can we agree on an extension contract across those layers rather than requiring each deployment platform to maintain its own runtime wrapper?

body_text:
## Motivation
Revisit nested skill-directory support for monorepos without overwhelming the agent prompt. This is a follow-up design task: reliable skill loading and reloading after repository discovery or cloning remain higher priority.

## Considerations
- Define discovery and scoping across nested directories, including how skills from different folders are represented and distinguished in the prompt.
- Design for scale: with 1,000 skills across 20 folders, avoid injecting metadata for every skill into the system prompt.
- Evaluate bounded skill-description prompt budgets and progressive or on-demand discovery, including how relevant skills are selected and omitted skills remain discoverable.
- Investigate Claude Code and Codex approaches to limiting skill-description prompt usage; validate their behavior rather than assuming a specific cap.

## Outcome
Document the proposed developer experience, discovery and scoping rules, and prompt-budget strategy before implementation.

Requested by @sydney-runkle.

## Request
Support non-blocking, provider-native async tool calling for arbitrary Deep Agents tools, not just background subagents. An agent should be able to launch a slow tool, continue independent work or conversation while it runs, and consume its result later.

This is distinct from Python async functions / `ainvoke`, parallel tool execution that still waits for all results, and background response generation.

## Provider support
- OpenAI documents first-class async tool calling in the Responses API: set `async: true` on a function or custom tool; the model can continue without its result, and the application returns the eventual output using the original `call_id`. The application remains responsible for execution and job management. See https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/async-tool-calling (including model compatibility restrictions).
- Anthropic: no equivalent general-purpose native non-blocking client-tool capability was found in the public documentation checked for this issue. Its documented client-tool protocol requires tool results immediately after the corresponding assistant tool-use message, with no intervening messages. Parallel tool use is not equivalent. See https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls . Revisit as provider capabilities evolve.

## Proposed scope
- Offer an explicit opt-in for general tools to run without blocking independent model work; do not infer this merely from an async Python implementation.
- Initially integrate supported OpenAI models, preserving async metadata and original call IDs through the model/tool adapters. Identify any prerequisite LangChain/LangGraph work.
- Track pending calls and deliver completed results to the correct conversation/call, including results that finish out of order or after intervening turns.
- Define lifecycle behavior for checkpoint/resume, errors, cancellation, timeouts, and agent completion with pending work; avoid duplicate execution/result delivery.
- Let the model explicitly wait when its next step depends on pending results.
- Keep the interface extensible to other providers. Document unsupported-provider behavior explicitly rather than silently treating blocking execution as native async support.
- Add focused tests and an example demonstrating a slow tool running while the agent completes independent work, followed by consumption of its delayed result.

## Motivation
Reduce latency for long-running lookups, external jobs, and user-input requests. OpenAI already exposes the native capability; a general interface would allow additional providers to be integrated as equivalent support becomes available.
